title_original: ‘Safe Exit’ Director Mohammed Hammad on Staying True to His Vision: ‘I Need to Be Free as a Filmmaker’
editorial_title_zh: 《安全出口》（Safe Exit）导演穆罕默德·哈马德谈坚守创作愿景：“作为一个电影人，我需要保持自由”
editorial_excerpt_zh: 穆罕默德·哈马德（Mohammed Hammad）的《安全出口》（Safe Exit）在2025年马拉喀什电影节阿特拉斯工作坊（Atlas Workshops）荣获后期制作阿特拉斯奖，随后在2026年柏林电影节全景单元首映。目前，该片正准备在埃尔古纳电影节（El Gouna Film Festival）迎来本土首映……

Bread）的电影。那是一个大项目，是一部公路片，Film Clinic 是制片方之一。但当我完成剧本（该剧本于2020年获得红海电影节阿拉伯项目红海之阁奖）并进行堪景时，影片遭到了审查部门的拒绝。于是，这个我倾注喜爱的项目在经历了4年的工作后戛然而止。那之后，我写不出东西了。但我给伟大的导演达乌德·阿卜杜勒-赛イド（Daoud Abdel Sayed）打了电话，他告诉我，去开启另一个项目，写另一部电影。起我现在对他说，这太难了，我现在的状态不行。但大约一个月后，我开始创作《安全出口》，剧本大约又花了一年时间才完成。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但你在《安全出口》中并没有走安全路线——片中有些内容可能也会让这里的审查部门不快。听着，作为一个电影人，我需要保持自由，表达我的观点，并选择我想探讨的主题。我们与审查办公室进行了长时间的讨论，也许这种讨论对电影产生了积极的影响。目前，他们已经批准我们在埃及国内的电影节上放映这部电影，埃尔古纳就是我们的国内首映。我非常感谢埃尔古纳电影节给予我们的支持：这里是埃及，是我的祖国，能够来到这里，对我以及我的演员和剧组而言都极其重要。他们相信这部电影，对我们来说这是一个绝佳的机会。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们来聊聊你的角色。片中有三位截然不同的主角：一个深陷创伤的科普特族年轻男子萨马安（Samaan）；一个看尽生活阴暗面的无家可归穆斯林女性法蒂玛（Fatimah）；以及一个伊斯兰恐怖分子阿卜杜拉（Abdullah）。我们先从科普特元素谈起。我爱我的角色，尤其是萨马安和法蒂玛。他们很纯粹，非常纯粹。关于科普特基督徒，埃及大约有1500万。他们当中许多人非常成功，并融入了社会，但鉴于其少数群体身份，他们当然也有特定的问题。但萨马安还有另一个问题：他的父亲在利比亚被 ISIS 杀害，因此他患上了慢性创伤后应激障碍（PTSD）。他试图应对所处的世界，但最重要的是，他试图面对自己和内心的恐惧。他无法处理自己的情感，这与法蒂玛截然相反，法蒂玛非常健谈且率性。她不识字且没有身份证明，尽管他们截然不同，但他们都处于社会的边缘。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你是如何安排这段排练时间的？第一要务是让他们习惯共同生活和交谈。让他们走在开罗市中心的街头，坐下来喝杯咖啡，培养出友谊。直到这时，我才开始和他们谈论故事和各自的角色。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": Exit》是一部非常沉重硬朗的影片，但在某些场景中，我们也加入了一些柔和感，特别是在涉及法蒂玛的时候。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管影片氛围沉重，你还是设法在这个非常严肃的故事里融入了一些幽默。我相信喜剧调剂（comic Exit》代表了现在的我。至于第三部电影会怎样，我目前还不知道[笑]。但我学到的是如何让人们感到引人入胜。因为就电影而言，保持趣味性依然很重要。尽管《Safe Exit》风格黑暗，且探讨了一个非常严肃、极其敏感的话题，但我们依然能让它的一部分内容充满观赏性！", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本采访经过编辑和删节以保持清晰流畅。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Mohammed Hammad ’s “Safe Exit” received an Atlas Prize for Post-production at the 2025 Atlas Workshops of the Marrakech Film Festival before making its debut in the Panorama section of the 2026 Berlinale. The film is now poised for its national debut at the El Gouna Film Festival , where it’s competing in the Feature Narrative section.

The film is Hammad’s long-awaited follow-up to his debut “Withered Green,” which bowed at the 2016 Locarno Film Festival and went on to win the best director prize at the Dubai Film Festival, as well as multiple awards closer to home in Cairo.

Related Stories

Hammad speaks to Variety about the challenges of getting his second film produced, and the satisfaction of screening in El Gouna.

Popular on Variety

How have you negotiated the difficulties of getting an independent film made in Egypt now? “Safe Exit” is completely self-funded. We formed a new production company, Pariedolia Productions, and now we’re trying to distribute the film through that company, which is a challenge. We’ve chosen this model because many studios in Egypt tend to avoid this kind of film, especially given the topics it covers. Even getting the necessary permissions to shoot the film was very hard. But together with my producer Kholoud Saad I knew I needed to make this film, just like we made “Withered Green.”

What about your co-producers? The main co-producer is Dora Bouchoucha with Nomadis Images, from Tunisia. And Ibrahim El-Battout, one of the godfathers of independent cinema in Egypt, is also a co-producer. Ibrahim was with me from the beginning, also as an adviser, and I trust him completely. We worked on pre-production together, in conjunction with Kholoud; Ibrahim is one of Egypt’s leading independent filmmakers, along with Khairy Beshara and Yousry Nasrallah, and he was with us throughout the shooting, every day.

“Withered Green” premiered in 2014. Can you talk about the challenges you’ve faced getting “Safe Exit” off the ground? After “Withered Green.” I began work on a film called “Bullets & Bread.” It was a big project, a road movie, with Film Clinic as one of the producers. But after I finished the script [which received the Red Sea Lodge Award for an Arab Project in 2020], and I was scouting locations, the film was rejected by the censors. So my lovely project came to a halt after four years of work. After that, I couldn’t write. But I called the great director Daoud Abdel Sayed, and he told me, start another project, write another film. At first, I told him, it’s too hard, I’m not good now. But after a month or so, I began to write “Safe Exit,” which took about another year to finish the script.

But you’re not playing safe with “Safe Exit” – there are things in the film that might displease the censors here too. Look, I need to be free as a filmmaker, to express my point of view and select topics I want to address. We had long discussions with the censorship office, and maybe this discussion impacted the film in a positive way. At the moment they’ve given us permission to screen the film in festivals within Egypt, and El Gouna is our national premiere. I’m so grateful for the support we’ve gotten from the El Gouna Film Festival: this is Egypt, it’s my country, and it’s extremely important for me as well as my cast and crew that we’re here. They believe in the film, and for us it’s a great opportunity.

Let’s talk about your characters. You have three very distinct main characters: a young Coptic man, Samaan, dealing with trauma; a homeless Muslim woman, Fatimah, who’s seen more than her fair share of life’s darker side; and Abdullah, an Islamic terrorist. Let’s start with the Coptic element. I love my characters, especially Samaan and Fatimah. They’re pure, very pure. Regarding Coptic Christians, there are about 15 million in Egypt. Many of them are very successful and are integrated into society but of course they have specific issues given their minority status. But Samaan has another issue: his father was slaughtered in Libya by ISIS, and consequently he suffers from chronic PTSD. He’s trying to cope with the world he lives in but most importantly he’s trying to face himself and his fear. He can’t deal with his feelings, which is the opposite of Fatimah, who’s very talkative and spontaneous. She’s illiterate and undocumented, and while they’re very different, they’re both on the margins of society.

Can you describe how you worked with the actors? Marwan Waleed, who stars as Samaan, is a relative newcomer who only appeared in one series. Noha Foad, who plays Fatimah, has been a close friend for years [she starred in Hammad’s 2010 short “Pale Red”]. We had nine months of rehearsal with the two of them.

How did you approach that rehearsal time? Number one was getting them used to living together and talking together. Having them walk down the streets in Downtown Cairo, sitting down for a coffee, developing a friendship. Only after this did I talk to them about the story and their characters.

But the most important thing for me in rehearsals is that they took place in the main locations where we shot. The last two months of rehearsals were in the actual locations, so the actors felt at home there.

The look of the film is quite different from “Withered Green,” which was also shot by Mohammed El Sharqawy. I’ve worked with Mohammad starting with our short films. We always work together. I like a tough look, a harsh look. It’s very close to a natural look, using available light sources. With “Safe Exit,” there are more colorful scenes because Fatimah’s character calls for colors. They act as a contrast to Samaan’s routine, his pallid room and his workspace. I’m drawn to this harsh texture, and “Safe Exit” is a very tough picture, but we also put some softness in certain scenes, especially with Fatimah.

Despite its toughness, you’ve managed to insert some humor into a very serious story. I believe in comic relief, because the film is very dark. Maybe we can put some smiles on an audience, especially with Fatimah, but also with Samaan, who’s like a robot.

How do you see that you’ve developed between “Withered Green” and now? I’m very happy with “Withered Green” and I’m very happy with “Safe Exit,” but “Withered Green” was me at that time of life and “Safe Exit” is me now. I don’t know about the third film [laughs]. But what I learned is how to make people feel entertained. Because with cinema it’s still important to be entertaining. Even though “Safe Exit” is dark, and addresses a very serious, very sensitive topic, we can still make part of it entertaining!

title_original: Walston, A New Space for Photography in the Scottish Hills
editorial_title_zh: 沃尔斯顿：苏格兰山脉中的全新摄影空间
editorial_excerpt_zh: 沃尔斯顿是由卡罗琳·凯恩顿（Caroline Kenyon）在苏格兰腹地的一座17世纪教堂内创立的全新摄影中心。这篇文章《沃尔斯顿：苏格兰山脉中的全新摄影空间》最初发布在《摄影之眼》杂志上。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为领先的美食摄影比赛——世界美食摄影大赛（World Food Photography Awards）的创始人，卡罗琳·凯恩顿通过一个长期以来的夙愿继续履行她对摄影的承诺：沃尔斯顿，一个位于苏格兰腹地17世纪教堂内的画廊。这是一场关于如何将这个独特场所打造成全新摄影目的地的访谈。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "能跟我们谈谈你与这座教堂的初次相遇吗？你是如何发现它的，是什么吸引了你？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在Covid-19大流行期间，我在伦敦和哥哥一起照顾年迈的母亲。傍晚时分，我会在网上浏览，发现苏格兰有许多乡村教堂正在出售。这重燃了我有一天能拥有一个属于自己的画廊空间的希望，这是我多年来的梦想。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当我能够回家时，我发现了一座待售的美丽教堂。我通过火车、公交车和出租车出行去实地看房，一看到它那壮丽的环境——孤零零地坐落在广阔彭特兰山脉（Pentland Hills）山谷边缘——我就觉得这是一个千载难逢的机会。除了扇窗户外，所有的窗户都被木板封上了，但这个地方仍然充满光线。它有一种强大而美丽的氛围。我在那里呆了15分钟，然后给中介打电话出价。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你如何改造这个空间，或者决定不去改造它，从而将一座17世纪的教堂变成摄影画廊“沃尔斯顿”？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "它经历了非常轻度的修复。我想保留我最初发现它时那种神奇的、“睡美人”般的氛围。这里没有电，也没有自来水，目前我也没有计划改变这一点。这里有两个空间：主要空间长达15米以上，构成了画廊，墙壁呈粉笔白；而小圣衣室将被刷成红色，变成一个温暖舒适的办公室。这座建筑如此独特，其环境也非同寻常：教堂墓地里有美丽的坟墓和纪念碑，没有令人不安的东西，只有宁静与可爱。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你在社交媒体上提到开幕就在几天之后。最后的筹备工作进展得怎么样？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一切都在加速推进！油漆工在马不停蹄地刷墙，我有一卷卷胶卷需要收集并带到爱丁堡进行冲洗和扫描，当地的高档艺术打印机将负责制作照片，我们还有装裱要做，等等。但这是一项非常激动人心的事业，整个当地社区的热情和支持让我真正为之动容。我住在附近比加（Biggar）镇的一家家族经营的酒吧里，每当我结束长途驱车走进去时，我都感到宾至如归。我希望人们也觉得这是他们自己的空间。这是一个需要悉心呵护和尊重的地方。我希望开幕式能成为对人们对这个美丽地方的热爱的一场真正的欢乐庆典，伴随着摄影、茶水和蛋糕。一个真正的派对。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "能跟我们多聊聊首场展览吗？它将与这个地方及其周边环境紧密相连。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对我来说，首展必须扎根于社区，这一点非常重要。因此，我接洽了比加及周边地区的男士 shed（Biggar & District Men’s Shed），提议为该组织的成员举办一场摄影工作坊，最终的成果将作为开幕展。我的摄影师儿子亨利建议，让这些男士们专注于拍摄他们同行在修理、制作和恢复物品时的双手，以保持主题和题裁的具体性，并且让他们使用胶卷拍摄，我非常喜欢这个主意。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你曾说过：“我一直想要一个空间来展示对我有意义、并且我认为对别人也很重要的作品。”这感觉像是一个艺术梦想成真吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我一生都在看照片。我的母亲是一位曾为《观察家报》（The Observer）和《泰晤士报》（The Times）撰稿的记者，自我很小的时候起，她就会让我看伟大摄影师简·鲍恩（Jane Bown）和斯诺登勋爵（Lord Snowdon）的作品。在我二十多岁时，编辑一本我称之为“低成本《国家地理》”的杂志时，我看过每个摄影师的作品集，并亲自挑选了所有的图片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我培养了自己的眼光和对影像的反应。那远在世界美食摄影大赛创立之前；该赛事现在已经进入第16个年头。我有幸坐在入围评审团中，看到每一张提交的图片，每年数以千计。我和经验丰富的同事们一起工作，从摄影师、创意总监到编辑，并从他们身上学到了很多东西。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你希望在这个空间里展示和创造什么？你对未来的展览已经有什么想法或计划了吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我有一长串未来潜在展览的名单！明年6月，我计划举办一场伟大花卉摄影师克莱夫·伯斯内尔（Clive Boursnell）的展览，展出小斯巴达（Little Sparta）的影像——这是苏格兰最著名的花园之一，由已故艺术家伊恩·汉密尔顿·芬利（Ian Hamilton Finlay）创作，它恰好就在山谷的另一侧。当我为这座教堂出价时，我并不知道它就在那里。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我正在收集那些我想要展示作品的摄影师的名字。我在各处寻找灵感，通过对话和偶然的相遇。有时，这些作品来自那些拥有非凡才华、却并不认为自己是摄影师的人。能够给予他们一点鼓励并提供一个展示作品的平台，是一件非常愉快的事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "还有一些主题：世界食品摄影大奖（World Food Photography Awards）将于2028年与达尔基斯摄影节（Photo Dalkeith）合作，这令人非常兴奋；我正计划在沃尔ston（Walston）举办一场以冰淇淋为主题的平行展览，展品将采用该大奖档案馆中的影像。冰淇淋是苏格兰的一大传统，这也与一个多世纪前定居苏格兰并开办冰淇淋店的意大利人历史息息相关，其中许多店铺至今犹存。这是将不同线索交织在一起的一种美妙方式。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Founder of the World Food Photography Awards, a leading food photography competition, Caroline Kenyon is pursuing her commitment to photography through a long-held ambition: Walston, a gallery housed in a 17th-century church in the heart of Scotland. An interview about turning this distinctive place into a new destination for photography.

Can you tell us about your first encounter with this church? How did you discover it, and what drew you to it?

During the Covid-19 pandemic, I was in London, looking after my elderly mother with my brother. In the evenings, I would browse online and discovered that many rural churches in Scotland were being put up for sale. It revived my hope of one day having a space in which to create a gallery, something I had dreamed of for many years.

When I was able to return home, I spotted a beautiful church for sale. I arranged a viewing, travelling by train, bus and taxi, and as soon as I saw its magnificent setting, standing alone at the edge of a valley in the vast Pentland Hills, I thought this was a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. All the windows except one were boarded up, yet the place was still filled with light. It had a powerful, beautiful atmosphere. I spent fifteen minutes there and called the agent to make an offer.

How did you adapt the space, or decide not to adapt it, to turn a 17th-century church into Walston, a photography gallery?

It has undergone very light restoration. I wanted to preserve the magical, Sleeping Beauty atmosphere it had when I first found it. There is no electricity or running water and, for now, I have no plans to change that. There are two spaces: the main one is over 15 metres long and forms the gallery, with chalk-white walls, while the small vestry will be painted red and become a warm, comfortable office. The building is so distinctive and its setting extraordinary: there are beautiful graves and monuments in the churchyard, nothing unsettling, just something peaceful and lovely.

You mention on social media that the opening is just days away. What do the final preparations look like?

Everything is gathering pace! The decorator is painting tirelessly, I have rolls of film to collect and take to Edinburgh for developing and scanning, the local fine-art printer will make the prints, we have framing to do, and much more. But it is such an exciting thing to undertake, and I am genuinely touched by the enthusiasm and support of the whole local community. I am staying in the nearby town of Biggar, in a family-run pub, and whenever I walk in after the long drive, I feel at home. I want people to feel that this is their space too. It is a place that needs to be treated with care and respect. And I hope the opening will be a truly joyful celebration of the affection people feel for a beautiful place, with photography, tea and cakes. A real party.

Can you tell us more about the first exhibition, which will be closely connected to the place and its surroundings?

It was very important to me that the inaugural exhibition should be rooted in the community. So I approached the Biggar & District Men’s Shed to propose a photography workshop for its members, with the resulting work forming the opening exhibition. It was Henry, my photographer son, who suggested that the men focus on their fellow members’ hands as they repair, make and restore things, to keep the subject and theme specific, and that they work on film, which I loved.

You have said, ‘I have always wanted a space to show work that matters to me and that I think will matter to others.’ Does this feel like an artistic dream coming true?

I have been looking at photographs all my life. My mother was a journalist who wrote for The Observer and The Times, and when I was very young she would show me photographs by the great Jane Bown and Lord Snowdon. When I was in my twenties, editing a magazine I described as a low-budget National Geographic, I saw every photographer’s portfolio and made all the picture selections myself.

I developed my eye and my responses to images. That was long before the World Food Photography Awards were established; they are now in their 16th year. I have the privilege of sitting on the shortlisting jury and seeing every image submitted, thousands each year. I work alongside experienced colleagues, from photographers and creative directors to editors, and have learned a great deal from them.

What would you like to show and create in this space? Do you already have ideas or plans for future exhibitions?

I have a long list of potential future exhibitions! Next June, I am planning an exhibition by Clive Boursnell, the great garden photographer, featuring images of Little Sparta, one of Scotland’s most celebrated gardens, created by the late artist Ian Hamilton Finlay, which happens to be just across the valley. I had no idea it was there when I made my offer on the church.

I am gathering the names of photographers whose work I would like to show. I find ideas everywhere, through conversations and chance encounters. And sometimes it is work by people with extraordinary talent who do not think of themselves as photographers. It is a great pleasure to give them a little encouragement and a platform to show their work.

There are themes too: the World Food Photography Awards will collaborate with Photo Dalkeith in 2028, which is very exciting, and I am planning a parallel exhibition at Walston devoted to ice cream, using images from the Awards’ archive. Ice cream is a great Scottish tradition, also connected to the history of Italians who settled in Scotland more than a century ago and opened ice cream businesses, many of which are still there today. A lovely way to bring different strands together.
excerpt_original: Walston is a new photographic center housed in a 17th-century church in the heart of Scotland founded by Caroline Kenyon. Cet article Walston, A New Space for Photography in the Scottish Hills est apparu en premier sur The Eye of Photography Magazine .

article_text:
Neon has partnered with Mayor Zohran Mamdani ’s office to host four free screenings of Once Upon a Time in Harlem across New York City this October.

The screenings will happen on Saturday, October 24, and Sunday, October 25, at AMC Magic Johnson Harlem, Film Forum, and Film at Lincoln Center. See the full screening schedule below. You can RSVP for the screenings here .

SCREENING SCHEDULE :

Saturday, October 24

Watch on Deadline

— 1:00 PM at AMC Magic Johnson Harlem , 2309 Frederick Douglass Blvd, New York, NY 10027

Related Stories

'NAZA' Tops $1 Million With Neon, Solid Limited Expansion For 'La Bola Negra' -- Specialty Box Office

Mayor Zohran Mamdani And Neon Set Free NYC Screenings Of 'Once Upon A Time In Harlem'

— 4:45 PM at Film Forum , 209 W Houston St, New York, NY 10014

Sunday, October 25

— 1:00 PM at AMC Magic Johnson Harlem , 2309 Frederick Douglass Blvd, New York, NY 10027

— 3:45 PM at Howard Gilman Theater, Film at Lincoln Center, 144 W 65th St, New York, NY 10023

“Once Upon a Time in Harlem brings the personalities, ideas, and debates behind the Harlem Renaissance to life for a new generation of New Yorkers,” Mayor Mamdani said of the film in a statement.

“We are proud to partner with the filmmaking team to offer free screenings to New Yorkers this weekend, ensuring that as many New Yorkers as possible get the chance to experience this film. Our city owes a debt of gratitude to the artists of the Harlem Renaissance whose enduring legacy is still felt in every jazz club, in every gallery, and in the movement for social justice that still continues to this day.”

The only film this year to screen at the Sundance, Cannes, Telluride, Toronto, and New York Film Festivals, Once Upon a Time in Harlem is nominated for five Critics Choice Documentary Awards, including Best Documentary. The film won the 2026 Library of Congress Lavine / Ken Burns Film Prize and the Maysles Film Center Albie Award.

Inventive in form, the film was conceived and filmed in 1972 by the late William Greaves. The film is shaped around a cocktail party Greaves hosted at Duke Ellington’s home in Harlem. Greaves invited every surviving creator of the Harlem Renaissance he could locate – many of whom had not seen one another in more than 50 years. For four hours, the group of artists laughed, drank, and debated their position in the rapidly shifting cultural landscape. Greaves filmed it all.

The footage was originally shot for a film about the Harlem Renaissance called From These Roots , which Greaves completed in 1974 using only archival materials. The interviews and discussions from the party were put to the side. However, Greaves, who went on to become a major figure of American independent cinema, completing over 70 films, including the now-seminal Symbiopsychotaxiplasm films, believed Once Upon a Time in Harlem was his greatest work. He spent much of the rest of his life wrestling with how to finish the film. He died in 2014, with the film incomplete. His widow, Louise Greaves, continued working on the project until she died in 2023, at which point his son, David Greaves, and David’s daughter, Liani Greaves, picked up the mantle. Film producer Anne de Mare oversaw the restoration and digitization of the footage used in the doc. We spoke with the team behind the film ahead of their world premiere at Sundance.

Neon picked up the film following the screening at Sundance, beating out Netflix and Mubi. The film was released earlier this month, in time for William Greaves’ centenary.

article_text:
ゴジラ－0.0

劇場公開日： 2026年11月3日

解説・あらすじ

第96回アカデミー賞でアジア映画として初の視覚効果賞を受賞するなど、世界的に大きな話題を集めた「ゴジラ－1.0」の続編。山崎貴が引き続き監督・脚本・VFXを担い、前作から2年後の世界を舞台に、再び姿を現したゴジラとの新たな戦いを描き出す。 戦争によって「無（ゼロ）」となった日本を、ゴジラが「負（マイナス）」に叩き落としてから2年。もがき苦しみながらも復興を遂げ、ようやく取り戻したはずの日常に、再びゴジラが襲いかかる。人々はこの戦いを終わらせるべく、総力を結集して新たな作戦に乗り出す。 キャストは、前作でゴジラと壮絶な死闘を繰り広げた主人公・敷島浩一役の神木隆之介、ゴジラに襲われながらも奇跡的に一命をとりとめたヒロイン・敷島典子役の浜辺美波をはじめ、山田裕貴、佐々木蔵之介、安藤サクラ、吉岡秀隆ら前作の顔ぶれが再集結。さらに新たなメンバーとして、気象台から大型災害対策事務局に出向した天才気象予報官・青山真琴役で長澤まさみ、戦争で心に深い傷を負った生物学者・村上寛治役で田中泯、医師・緒方役で國村隼が出演。

2026年製作／135分／G／日本 配給：東宝 劇場公開日：2026年11月3日

article_text:
NYC Weekend Watch is our weekly round-up of repertory offerings.

Film at Lincoln Center Ken Russell’s reconstructed The Devils has begun playing on a restored 35mm print—read (or listen to) our interview with Mark Kermode on it.

Roxy Cinema A program of Michel Auder’s works and 30th-anniversary screening of Karishika play on Sunday.

Museum of Modern Art Films by Chantal Akerman screen in a Claire Atherton retrospective .

BAM Ken Russell’s reconstructed The Devils has begun playing—read (or listen to) our interview with Mark Kermode on it.

Film Forum An Andrzej Wajda series continues; Spy Kids shows on Sunday.

Anthology Film Archives Films by Eisenstein screen in Essential Cinema .

Museum of the Moving Image A Michael Cocoyannis retrospective runs this weekend; Fantasia and Murnau’s Faust also play.

IFC Center Ken Russell’s reconstructed The Devils has begun playing on a restored 35mm print—read (or listen to) our interview with Mark Kermode on it—while The Exorcist , The House with Laughing Windows , and Redline play late.

Nitehawk Prospect Park The Addams Family and a print of Vampire’s Kiss screen early on Saturday and Sunday.

Metrograph Midnight in Paris , Strangers on a Train , and The Aristocats show on 35mm while Paris is a Woman starts showing in a restoration; Oleksandr Dovzhenko , Trains: Local Routes , Classical Cinema , and Darius Khondji continue.

"“InSitu2”作为一个旨在促进当代创作的共同项目，连接了东京、慕尼黑和北京的路易威登空间。它被定位为路易威登长期以来对艺术持续开展的举措的一部分。在2015年的“IN SITU-1”中，巴黎、东京和慕尼黑的场馆首次联动，以“地域性”为主题聚焦女性艺术家。这一次，项目邀请了扎根于各个城市的艺术家，围绕各自城市的创意现场展开独特的项目。会展期间将举办表演、对谈活动以及参与式项目，成为艺术家、表演者、作家和地方社群探索文化交流与变迁形态的场所。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/5661f9a2/6e535adb-7d08-4a3e-a1a5-5bf6b11596e4.jpg?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "“InSitu2 – Ibasho（居場所）”路易威登东京路易威登空间展场风貌（2026）　Photo "东京的主题是“居場所”（归属之地）。项目不仅局限于物理空间，更探讨空间如何因其中进行的活动、反复的日常劳作、共享的时间以及被唤起的记忆而发生转变。展场并非仅仅用于欣赏作品的场所，而是作为来客可以停留度过时光的场地对外开放，并迎接有着不同背景的人们。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/993b6d4b/48f3696b-c109-4f76-9b71-2253f21dfc70.jpg?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "“InSitu2 – Ibasho（居場所）”路易威登东京路易威登空间展场风貌（2026）　Photo "活动由丰富多样的形式构成。例如，表演活动包括以归属地为主题的落语、脱离传统舞台上演的能剧，以及探讨音乐中“归属”感的DJ与即兴演奏。此外，还将举办嘉宾对谈活动以及将归属地作为社会命题探讨的文学聚会。作为教育项目，这里备有面向各个年龄段参与者的工作坊和电影放映会，每周日还会举办儿童工作坊。即使是没有活动的日期，来客也可以造访展场，体验空间本身。阅读、小憩或是与其他来客交流，来客可以根据各自的喜好自由滞留，这也是本项目的特征。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/98ef6f87/c9b77635-e5a4-4421-bc8b-2bc91416b1a3.jpg?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "“InSitu2 "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/0badccd9/9fc9cf25-ea74-4975-9f95-01262a566df2.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "“InSitu2 – Ibasho（居場所）”路易威登东京路易威登空间展场风貌（2026）　Photo credits: © "踏入其中，来客会仿佛回到童年一般，抬头仰望巨大的家具。暖炉桌、壁橱、电视、椅子，以及向露台延伸出去的桌子。在窗帘的背面，甚至还有一个可以藏身的空间。一边兜兜转转地走动，一边寻找对自己而言舒适地点的这段时光本身就充满乐趣。据说，每一件家具的灵感都源自持续描绘日本日常生活与家庭的电影导演小津安二郎的作品中出现的道具。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "会场深处设置了书架，项目参与者挑选的书籍琳琅满目地排列其上。任何人都可以拿起来在现场阅读。平时不对外开放的露台也将开放，能够欣赏到从路易威登东京路易威登空间眺望的城市风光，这也是一大看点。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/27a7206e/46b631d4-150e-410d-b939-124c6bc2eef9.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "能剧表演　摄影：作者", "credit": "Tokyo Art ルイ・ヴィトンを結ぶプロジェクト。ルイ・ヴィトンが芸術に対して長年続けてきた取り組みの一環に位置づけられる。2015年の「IN SITU-1」では、パリ、東京、ミュンヘンの会場が初めて連携し、「地域性」を主題に女性アーティストを取り上げた。今回は各都市に拠点を置くアーティストを招き、それぞれの都市のクリエイティブなシーンを題材にした独自のプロジェクトを展開する。会期中にはパフォーマンスやトークイベント、参加型プログラムが行われ、アーティストやパフォーマー、作家、地域のコミュニティが、文化的な交流や変容の在り方を探る場となる。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/5661f9a2/6e535adb-7d08-4a3e-a1a5-5bf6b11596e4.jpg?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "「InSitu2 – "東京のテーマは「居場所」。物理的な空間にとどまらず、そこで行われる行為や繰り返される所作、共有される時間、呼び起こされる記憶によって空間が変化する様を扱う。会場は作品を鑑賞するための場ではなく、来場者が滞在して過ごせる場として開かれ、異なる背景を持つ人々を迎え入れる。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/993b6d4b/48f3696b-c109-4f76-9b71-2253f21dfc70.jpg?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "「InSitu2 – Ibasho（居場所）」エスパスルイ･ヴィトン東京での展示風景（2026）　Photo "アクティビティは多様な形式で構成される。たとえば、パフォーマンスでは、居場所をテーマにした落語、伝統的な舞台を離れて上演される能、音楽における「居場所」の感覚を扱うDJやジャムセッションが行われる。このほか、ゲストによるトークイベントや、社会的な問いとして居場所を扱う文芸の集いを開く。教育プログラムとして、世代を問わず参加できるワークショップや映画上映会があり、毎週日曜日には子供向けワークショップが実施される。イベントのない日にも会場を訪れることができ、空間そのものを体験できる。読書や休息、ほかの来場者との交流など、来場者はそれぞれの過ごし方で自由に滞在できるのが本プログラムの特徴だ。"}, 3都市をつなぐ「InSitu2」プログラム

表参道の エスパス ルイ･ヴィトン東京 にて、 「InSitu2 – Ibasho（居場所）」 と題したプログラムが開催される。会期は10月24日から11月27日まで。

「InSitu2」は、現代のクリエーションを促進する共通のプログラムとして、東京、ミュンヘン、北京のエスパス ルイ・ヴィトンを結ぶプロジェクト。ルイ・ヴィトンが芸術に対して長年続けてきた取り組みの一環に位置づけられる。2015年の「IN SITU-1」では、パリ、東京、ミュンヘンの会場が初めて連携し、「地域性」を主題に女性アーティストを取り上げた。今回は各都市に拠点を置くアーティストを招き、それぞれの都市のクリエイティブなシーンを題材にした独自のプロジェクトを展開する。会期中にはパフォーマンスやトークイベント、参加型プログラムが行われ、アーティストやパフォーマー、作家、地域のコミュニティが、文化的な交流や変容の在り方を探る場となる。

東京のテーマは「居場所」。物理的な空間にとどまらず、そこで行われる行為や繰り返される所作、共有される時間、呼び起こされる記憶によって空間が変化する様を扱う。会場は作品を鑑賞するための場ではなく、来場者が滞在して過ごせる場として開かれ、異なる背景を持つ人々を迎え入れる。

アクティビティは多様な形式で構成される。たとえば、パフォーマンスでは、居場所をテーマにした落語、伝統的な舞台を離れて上演される能、音楽における「居場所」の感覚を扱うDJやジャムセッションが行われる。このほか、ゲストによるトークイベントや、社会的な問いとして居場所を扱う文芸の集いを開く。教育プログラムとして、世代を問わず参加できるワークショップや映画上映会があり、毎週日曜日には子供向けワークショップが実施される。イベントのない日にも会場を訪れることができ、空間そのものを体験できる。読書や休息、ほかの来場者との交流など、来場者はそれぞれの過ごし方で自由に滞在できるのが本プログラムの特徴だ。

会期中に変化する「居場所」

大きなリビングルームに見立てた会場の空間構成を手がけたのは、日本の若手建築家コレクティヴ「GROUP」だ。本プロジェクトのアクティビティや制作パートナーと連携しながら、会期を通じて表情を変え続ける空間を作り上げ、エスパス ルイ・ヴィトン東京の中に「居場所」を立ち上げた。

足を踏み入れると、来場者はまるで子供に戻ったかのように、大きな家具を見上げることになる。こたつ、押し入れ、テレビ、椅子、そしてテラスへとせり出すテーブル。カーテンの裏には、身をひそめられる空間もある。ぐるぐると歩き回りながら、自分にとって居心地の良い場所を探す時間そのものが楽しい。それぞれの家具は、日本の日常や家庭を描き続けた映画監督・小津安二郎の作品に登場するものから着想を得ているという。

会場の奥には本棚が据えられ、プログラムの参加者が選んだ本がずらりと並ぶ。誰でも手に取り、その場で読むことができる。普段は開放されていないテラスにも出られ、エスパス ルイ・ヴィトン東京から望む街の景色を楽しめるのも見どころだ。

開幕に先立ち、能のプログラムの一部が披露された。大きな窓の向こうに広がる都市の風景を背に演じられる能は、この会場でしか出会えない光景だ。外出が心地よい秋の一日、腰を落ち着けにふらりと訪れてみてはいかがだろうか。

article_text:
Hong Sangsoo ’s “ Nowhere to Lay My Eyes ,” a triple prizewinner at the 79th Locarno Film Festival, and Kim Jin-yu’s “ Journey There ,” the first Korean production to star “Beef” actor Justin H. Min , have picked up a new batch of territory deals through Seoul-based sales outfit Finecut.

For “Nowhere to Lay My Eyes,” Carlotta Films has taken France, Mimosa Films has Japan, Kligger has Argentina and The Stone and the Plot has Portugal. The new pacts add to earlier sales to The Cinema Guild for North America, Filmgarten for Austria, Hugoeast for China, Atalante for Spain, Cola Films for Taiwan and the Institute of Contemporary Arts for the U.K.

Related Stories

New 'Naruto' Anime Series and 'Shadow Rising' Manga Revealed

'Avatar: Seven Havens' Renewed for Seasons 3 and 4 at Paramount+

The film is Hong’s 35th feature. At Locarno it won best direction, best performance and the Ecumenical Jury Prize. It sees the director team up again with regulars Kim Minhee (“By the Stream”) and Kwon Haehyo (“What Does That Nature Say to You”), and marks his first outing with Choi Myeonggil, whose credits include TV series “Durian’s Affair.” Jeonwonsa Film Co. produced.

“Journey There” has sold to Andrews Film for Taiwan, KDDI Corporation for Japan, Lev Cinema for Israel and Izagur Media for Mongolia, while Kairos Distribution acquired inflight rights. The drama centers on a middle-aged widow who begins getting ready for her own journey and gets drawn into relationships she never saw coming in the apartment she has just moved into.

Min’s credits include Kogonada’s “After Yang” and the Netflix series “Beef” and “The Umbrella Academy.” The film is the second feature from Kim, whose first, “Bori,” took two prizes at the 24th Schlingel International Film Festival. Kim’s own company, Pado, produced.

“Journey There” was released in Korea on Oct. 28. It has been invited to the Moscow International Film Festival, the New York Asian Film Festival and, more recently, the Paris and London Korean film festivals.

Fresh from Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market, Finecut heads to AFM with a slate that includes the animated “Long Long Night.” The film will screen there for buyers for the first time in its English-dubbed version. It also has invitations from Toronto, Busan and Sitges under its belt.

Also on offer are “Dora,” selected for Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight and Busan’s Gala Presentation section, and “Wi-Fi Love in the Palace,” a period fantasy romance toplined by Kim Young-hoon of K-pop group The Boyz.

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "As 2026 winds down, like most cinephiles, we’re looking to get our eyes on titles that may have slipped through the cracks or simply gone unseen, so—as we do each year—we’re sharing a rundown of the best titles available to watch at home."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Curated from the Best Films of 2026 So Far list we published for the first half of the year, it also includes films we’ve enjoyed the past few months and some with which we’ve recently caught up. In the meantime, see our rundown below, and be sure to catch up on recommended theatrical releases here .", "links": [{"text": "our weekly column", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/tag/new-to-streaming"}, {"text": "here", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/the-best-movies-now-playing-in-theaters/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "28 Years Later: The Bone Temple (Nia DaCosta)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/28-Years-Later-The-Bone-Temple-1-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple , the Jimmy gang is back, led by Jack O’Connell in a role that oddly mirrors his Irish vampire villain in last year’s Sinners . They’ve taken Spike (Alfie Williams), the pre-teen protagonist of the previous entry, now separated from his parents, under their wing. They ended the last film saving Spike’s life from the infected, but it’s soon revealed they have nefarious means to install themselves as new leaders of a post-apocalyptic society, among them the brutal torture of any other survivors who won’t conform. The rather unpleasant violence in these sequences is a different beast than all the goofy spine-ripping (still here) of Boyle’s predecessor. – Ethan V. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/28-years-later-the-bone-temple-review-stripped-down-sequel-still-infects-charm/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where to Stream: Netflix , VOD", "links": [{"text": "Netflix", "url": "https://www.netflix.com/search?q=bone%20temple&jbv=82622299"}, {"text": "VOD", "url": "https://amzn.to/4tFewzl"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Blue Film (Elliot Tuttle)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Blue-Film-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Provocation” has become watered-down in recent times. All it takes to provoke someone is tossing off a bunch of half-assed offensive statements or aiming your cannon at every divisive mainstream issue on a quest to push people’s buttons. Getting a reaction out of people is easy; actually making them consider things is another matter entirely. Blue Film , by that token, is provocative in the truest sense of the term. Elliott Tuttle’s film seeks to unsettle, question, and, yes, provoke you. But his masterful two-hander wants, more than anything, to extend understanding to both men at the center, asking you to see them as flawed humans with depth and complexity, even if we’d rather not. – Devan S. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/blue-film-review-masterful-two-hander-confronts-flaws-with-empathy/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where to Stream: VOD", "links": [{"text": "VOD", "url": "https://link.amazon/B04sJY33z"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Blue Heron (Sophy Romvari)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Blue-Heron-2-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Blue Heron , Romvari’s feature debut, once again mines the director’s own history, following a Hungarian family of six as it settles in a nondescript stretch of suburbia outside Vancouver. The opening line, “I struggle now to remember much of my childhood,” belongs to the youngest child, Sasha (Eylul Guven), the film to her older stepbrother Jeremy (Edik Beddoes), a sullen, taciturn adolescent with a history of self-destructive behavior no one has learned how to deal with, much less address. Yet Romvari refuses to write him off as a troubled child. Yes, the kid is most certainly not all right, but he traverses Blue Heron as its most mysterious, elusive character, and that impenetrability is a measure of Romvari’s empathy. Rather than pathologizing his pain––a tendency his own parents succumb to––she invites us to sit with it and bask in his drawn-out silences, in the gaps between the words and imperfect memories that grown-up Sasha (Amy Zimmer), in the film’s second half, will try piecing together. – Leonardo G. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/locarno-review-a-seance-of-self-and-film-blue-heron-is-an-astonishing-debut/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where to Stream: The Criterion Channel , VOD", "links": [{"text": "The Criterion Channel", "url": "https://www.criterionchannel.com/films/dYoRFiz7/blue-heron"}, {"text": "VOD", "url": "https://link.amazon/A03ZIE1HQ"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Coyote vs. Acme (Dave Green)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Coyote-vs-Acme-1200x497.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The first sign that we’re in good hands comes right at the start. One of the script’s earliest character introductions is—of all people—Peter Lorre. In this world, he’s a scientist at the Acme Corporation (not to be confused with the grocery chain) evading security guards with a variety of nefarious devices like Expanding Boulders and Large Magnets. The second sign of quality is the law firm handling the titular court case: Avery, Jones, and Maltese. It’s the kind of naming convention that could only come from a creative team with a deep reverence not just for the Looney Tunes, but the medium of animation itself. – Devan S. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/coyote-vs-acme-review-a-resurrected-comedy-that-delivers/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where to Stream: VOD", "links": [{"text": "VOD", "url": "https://link.amazon/B0fZSUyIA"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Currents (Milagros Mumenthaler)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/The-Currents-1200x645.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Writer-director Milagros Mumenthaler paints an intimate portrait of a woman trying to reckon with her fractured identity, trying not to fall into the grip of madness. Mumenthaler understands that motherhood requires an element of performance that reminds the mother that her life is no longer hers alone. Though the love for her daughter is still there inside, she cowers from it, preoccupied with inspecting the current shape of her life. In therapy, Lina expresses a fear of water’s power and the strength of a current that could wash her away. It’s as if she now knows the fragility of her existence, and that the confidence that once governed her was washed away when she jumped off the bridge. Despite the eccentricity of her fears, the emotions behind them are painfully relatable to any woman who feels that the inertia of her life has taken over. – Jourdain S. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/nyff-review-the-currents-is-an-intimate-portrait-of-fractured-identity/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where to Stream: Kino Film Collection , VOD", "links": [{"text": "Kino Film Collection", "url": "https://kinofilmcollection.com/"}, {"text": "VOD", "url": "https://link.amazon/A0aWrJcYr"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Disclosure Day (Steven Spielberg)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Disclosure-Day-1-1200x676.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Certain beliefs unite all of humanity. Take, for example, the idea that the extraordinary is possible. Or, even more, that the impossible is possible. Steven Spielberg isn’t shy about believing in extraterrestrial life, and he doesn’t think you should be either. He’s so sincere about this aloof-yet-sky-high-stakes concept that he’s returning to it again with a very simple profundity in tow: “Empathy is the core of animate existence–our evolutionary advantage.” And he intends to remind us of our capacity for such. – Luke H. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/disclosure-day-review-a-soul-searching-spine-tingling-blockbuster-triumph/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where to Stream: Peacock , VOD", "links": [{"text": "Peacock", "url": "https://www.peacocktv.com/stream-movies/disclosure-day"}, {"text": "VOD", "url": "https://link.amazon/A0iD1EilG"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Dry Leaf (Alexandre Koberidze)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Dry-Leaf-1200x901.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Languorous without becoming laborious, meditative without becoming meandering, abstract without becoming abstruse, Alexandre Koberidze’s Dry Leaf is a road movie unlike any other. It follows Irakli (David Koberidze), a father in search of his daughter, a sports photographer whose sudden disappearance is less of an enigma to solve than a vehicle for Koberidze’s imagination to serenely drift. Featuring Giorgi Koberidze’s charming, addictive score and shot on a Sony Ericsson, the fuzzy look of which transforms mundane landscapes into foreign-seeming textural images and hypnotic sequences, Dry Leaf , at 186 minutes, actively heightens our perception to its bucolic territory, its singular wavelength. It’s the kind of film where the destination is less important than the journey, where submission to its logic is more meaningful than a resistance, and where, like a vivid dream, its numinous sensations linger long after viewing. No matter the resolution, Koberidze has established himself as a modern enchanter. – Nirris N."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where to Stream: MUBI", "links": [{"text": "MUBI", "url": "https://mubi.com/ifsn"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "EPiC: Elvis Presley in Concert (Baz Luhrmann)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Elvis-Presley-1200x676.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In a way, EPiC is the most naturalistic film Luhrmann’s ever made, unconventionally employing the traditional layout of a tell-all music doc. But that’s a misnomer under the singular, kinetic eye of the Moulin Rouge and Romeo + Juliet director, who brings a dazzling energy—as show-stopping in cinematic terms as The King’s concerts were in the musical—to the well-worn documentary style that electrifies the viewer into a state of ecstasy from start to finish. – Luke H. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/epic-elvis-presley-in-concert-review-baz-luhrmanns-ecstatic-tribute-to-the-king/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where to Stream: Paramount+ , VOD", "links": [{"text": "Paramount+", "url": "https://www.paramountplus.com/movies/video/ALVE01KP70AKRDE00TWZEJ2GW33HHP/"}, {"text": "VOD", "url": "https://link.amazon/B0bKAXA9p"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Fence (Claire Denis)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/The-Fence-film-1200x674.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Claire Denis’ The Fence is perhaps not so evocative and penetrating as her career high marks, but it’s stuck with me far more than most of the past year’s most “acclaimed” films. Ethan Vestby said in his review , “Is the idea of a Claire Denis film changing? There was likely an image one formed in their head when that name emerged: elliptical, sexy, avant-garde. Yet recent works are suggesting a different direction, one far more direct and less mysterious. It can even be said that her newest, The Fence , plays like a final film––not necessarily as a grand summation or statement, but like a stripping-down of almost everything possible.”", "links": [{"text": "his review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/tiff-review-claire-denis-the-fence-takes-an-unnerving-stare-into-darkness/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where to Stream: AMC+ , VOD", "links": [{"text": "AMC+", "url": "https://www.amcplus.com/"}, {"text": "VOD", "url": "https://link.amazon/B0eZxDSfs"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Fiume o morte! (Igor Bezinović)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Fiume-o-Morte-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Learning about Gabriele D’Annunzio’s 16-month occupation of Fiume, a tale vividly retold in Igor Bezinović’s new, Tiger Award-winning documentary Fiume o Morte! , I spared a thought for Yukio Mishima. D’Annunzio’s life didn’t end so theatrically, but the two men––celebrated writers and hyper-nationalists with hubristic military dreams and similarly contested legacies––certainly shared a taste for the quixotic and chaotic. Was D’Annunzio a fascist colonizer, as those who still remember him in Fiume (now Rijeka, Croatia) claim, or was he the admirable dreamer as romantic as his poems? A century later, the jury’s still out. – Rory O. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/rotterdam-review-tiger-winning-fiume-o-morte-is-a-historical-reenactment-of-rare-wit-and-energy/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where to Stream: VOD", "links": [{"text": "VOD", "url": "https://link.amazon/A09D9p7iV"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Invite (Olivia Wilde)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/The_Invite-Still_1-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Small in scale, yet so much greater than the sum of its parts, Wilde conducts her quartet of players to an orchestral performance. She builds the dramatic tension of a relationship-turned-powder-keg from years of complacency and poor communication over staccato strings until it reaches its summit, only for it to drop and rise again. Employing just four principal actors, including herself, and a single apartment, it’s an impressive feat to pull off and a testament to her progression as actor-turned-director. – Kent M. W. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/sundance-review-the-invite-is-a-knockout-relationship-comedy/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where to Stream: HBO Max (starting Friday) , VOD", "links": [{"text": "HBO Max", "url": "https://play.hbomax.com/movie/fa938c47-f857-4c06-b425-7e5cb2d8bb0a"}, {"text": "VOD", "url": "https://link.amazon/A0hs8cVoO"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Is God Is (Aleshea Harris)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Is-God-Is-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Complicated” doesn’t begin to describe the family history that twin sisters Racine (Kara Young) and Anaia (Mallori Johnson) are facing in Is God Is , Aleshea Harris’ film adaptation of her acclaimed play. A directorial debut brimming with storytelling ingenuity and stylistic verve, the revenge tale follows the sisters on their path toward justice after their father left them and their mother for dead. While sometimes the theatrics at play can take away from the desired emotional connection, it’s quite an impressive first outing in the directorial chair for Harris, hopefully leading to more opportunities. – Jordan R."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where to Stream: Prime Video, VOD", "links": [{"text": "Prime Video, VOD", "url": "https://amzn.to/3QhInyS"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Last One for the Road (Francesco Sossai)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Last-One-for-the-Road-1-1-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It doesn’t take long to work out where you are in The Last One for the Road ––for the backroads of Veneto, Italy, Francesco Sossai’s delightful new movie has the unmistakable specificity of a life spent there. What you instead start to wonder is the when of it all. The protagonists are a pair of rogues in their 50s––one of whom, Doriano (Pierpaolo Capovilla), wears a shirt the color of a tobacco stain, the other, Carlobianchi (Sergio Romano), a style of bushy mustache I’ve rarely seen onscreen since Bruno Ganz sported a similar one in The American Friend. Only after stumbling into a group of Gen Z students––the most visible dressed in the headgear of an Egyptian goddess––late at night along a Venice canal do we realize that our heroes exist in the here and now. If it wasn’t for their innate knack for catching last orders, regardless of the watering hole, you’d almost call them men out of time. – Rory O. ( full review)", "links": [{"text": "full review)", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/last-one-for-the-road-review-a-delightful-trip-through-italy/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where to Stream: The Criterion Channel , VOD", "links": [{"text": "The Criterion Channel", "url": "https://www.criterionchannel.com/films/ie7lqmcm/the-last-one-for-the-road"}, {"text": "VOD", "url": "https://link.amazon/A051ixO4O"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Maddie’s Secret (John Early)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Maddies-Secret-1200x800.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "You can’t accuse John Early of not committing. Through the majority of his acting career, the comedian has become a reliable avatar for a palpable, toxic, hilarious narcissism, playing characters oblivious to the world outside the bubbles they’ve so thoroughly cultivated. That was particularly evident over four seasons of Search Party , as well as last year’s Stress Positions , a Sundance favorite that exposed the absurdity of living in quarantine over a masked summer. As an agoraphobic tenant in a Brooklyn brownstone, Early took the situation’s disaster and approached it through his very specific kind of self-assured, righteous mania to such an extent that his freak-outs are still rattling around in my brain. – Jake K-S. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/tiff-review-maddies-secret-showcases-john-earlys-total-commitment/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where to Stream: VOD", "links": [{"text": "VOD", "url": "https://link.amazon/A0gKq2TUU"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Miroirs No. 3 (Christian Petzold)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Miroirs-No-3-1200x650.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "One of the greatest directors working today, Christian Petzold returned this year with another masterfully enigmatic, gripping drama. Luke Hicks said in his Cannes review , “ Miroirs No. 3 is the kind of work best-served with as little information as possible. It’s not among Petzold’s greatest, but films like Barbara and Undine have made that a very high bar to clear. It’s textbook Petzold, which I mean as a major compliment. Don’t expect all of the mysteries to be uncovered. There is no big explainer moment or narratively satisfying closure, the likes of which Petzold rejects, but the enigmas that do reveal themselves yield rare treasures.”", "links": [{"text": "his Cannes review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/cannes-review-christian-petzolds-mirrors-no-3-is-an-enigmatic-drama-about-letting-go/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where to Stream: MUBI , VOD", "links": [{"text": "MUBI", "url": "https://mubi.com/ifsn"}, {"text": "VOD", "url": "https://link.amazon/A08Unn57j"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Night Nurse (Georgia Bernstein)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/NIGHT-NURSE-Cemre-Paksoy-Bruce-McKenzie-1-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "We know so little about the life of Eleni (Cemre Paksoy), a nurse working in an upscale retirement community, until something awakens in her. Directed by Georgia Bernstein, the perverse Night Nurse doesn’t quite qualify as a psychosexual thriller, despite underlying erotic tension; there is something more seductive and sinister under the surface. – John F. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/sundance-review-night-nurse-is-a-perverse-seductive-thriller/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where to Stream: AMC+ , VOD", "links": [{"text": "AMC+", "url": "https://www.amcplus.com/"}, {"text": "VOD", "url": "https://amzn.to/4gbDvUS"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie (Matt Johnson)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Nirvanna-the-Band-the-Show-the-Movie-1200x662.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The funniest, most unpredictable, “no, seriously, how the fuck did they do that???” movie of the year is about two guys, an RV, and a dream to play the Rivoli. Matt Johnson and Jay McCarroll’s big screen take on their cult-classic web (and later cable) series is perfectly legible for newbies, throwing off enough gags across the spectrum that something will land, be it a particular movie seen in a theater to a stray comment from a passerby. As much a triumph of low-budget/mockumentary filmmaking as it is one of sheer audacity, it simply must be seen to be believed. – Devan S. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/nirvanna-the-band-the-show-the-movie-review-an-ambitious-comedic-triumph/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where to Stream: Hulu , VOD", "links": [{"text": "Hulu", "url": "https://www.hulu.com/series/94580421-e6d2-4d51-914f-e4faab6aa350"}, {"text": "VOD", "url": "https://link.amazon/A0aQ6OzzQ"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Our Land (Nuestra Tierra) (Lucrecia Martel)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/landmarks-lucrecia-martel-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "There is a direct and conscious through-line between Lucrecia Martel’s previous historical film Zama to her contemporary legal documentary Nuestra Tierra . We see the lives of indigenous communities in Argentina continue to be treated with little regard and a clear class and racial fissure exists in the nation. Martel films the court scenes and the footage of the disputed land as two battlegrounds spanning time. The murder of the Chuchagasta indigenous community leader Javie Chocobar at the hands of corrupt businessmen and bureaucrats reflects and mirrors the history of Argentina as, to this day, a disputed territory. While Martel’s cinema is known for its heavy use of metaphor, blending of fantasy and realism with impressionistic camerawork, this is a movie that pares everything down to cinema’s base elements, making crystal clear what is at stake. – Soham G."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where to Stream: The Criterion Channel , VOD", "links": [{"text": "The Criterion Channel", "url": "https://www.criterionchannel.com/films/rs6Ug3FX/our-land"}, {"text": "VOD", "url": "https://link.amazon/A02HhUkVz"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Remake (Ross McElwee)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Remake.png", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Though best-known for his landmark reflexive documentary Sherman’s March , Ross McElwee crafted his most aching, personal film yet with Remake , one of the very best films of 2026. article_text:
As 2026 winds down, like most cinephiles, we’re looking to get our eyes on titles that may have slipped through the cracks or simply gone unseen, so—as we do each year—we’re sharing a rundown of the best titles available to watch at home.

Curated from the Best Films of 2026 So Far list we published for the first half of the year, it also includes films we’ve enjoyed the past few months and some with which we’ve recently caught up. While our year-end coverage is still to come, including our staff’s top 50 films of 2026, this streaming guide will hopefully be a helpful tool for readers to have a chance to find notable––perhaps underseen––titles of late.

Note that we’re going by 2026 U.S. releases and that streaming services are limited solely to the territory as well. If you want to stay up-to-date with new titles being made available in the coming months, check out our weekly column . In the meantime, see our rundown below, and be sure to catch up on recommended theatrical releases here .

28 Years Later: The Bone Temple (Nia DaCosta)

In 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple , the Jimmy gang is back, led by Jack O’Connell in a role that oddly mirrors his Irish vampire villain in last year’s Sinners . They’ve taken Spike (Alfie Williams), the pre-teen protagonist of the previous entry, now separated from his parents, under their wing. They ended the last film saving Spike’s life from the infected, but it’s soon revealed they have nefarious means to install themselves as new leaders of a post-apocalyptic society, among them the brutal torture of any other survivors who won’t conform. The rather unpleasant violence in these sequences is a different beast than all the goofy spine-ripping (still here) of Boyle’s predecessor. – Ethan V. ( full review )

Where to Stream: Netflix , VOD

Blue Film (Elliot Tuttle)

“Provocation” has become watered-down in recent times. All it takes to provoke someone is tossing off a bunch of half-assed offensive statements or aiming your cannon at every divisive mainstream issue on a quest to push people’s buttons. Getting a reaction out of people is easy; actually making them consider things is another matter entirely. Blue Film , by that token, is provocative in the truest sense of the term. Elliott Tuttle’s film seeks to unsettle, question, and, yes, provoke you. But his masterful two-hander wants, more than anything, to extend understanding to both men at the center, asking you to see them as flawed humans with depth and complexity, even if we’d rather not. – Devan S. ( full review )

Where to Stream: VOD

Blue Heron (Sophy Romvari)

Blue Heron , Romvari’s feature debut, once again mines the director’s own history, following a Hungarian family of six as it settles in a nondescript stretch of suburbia outside Vancouver. The opening line, “I struggle now to remember much of my childhood,” belongs to the youngest child, Sasha (Eylul Guven), the film to her older stepbrother Jeremy (Edik Beddoes), a sullen, taciturn adolescent with a history of self-destructive behavior no one has learned how to deal with, much less address. Yet Romvari refuses to write him off as a troubled child. Yes, the kid is most certainly not all right, but he traverses Blue Heron as its most mysterious, elusive character, and that impenetrability is a measure of Romvari’s empathy. Rather than pathologizing his pain––a tendency his own parents succumb to––she invites us to sit with it and bask in his drawn-out silences, in the gaps between the words and imperfect memories that grown-up Sasha (Amy Zimmer), in the film’s second half, will try piecing together. – Leonardo G. ( full review )

Where to Stream: The Criterion Channel , VOD

Coyote vs. Acme (Dave Green)

The first sign that we’re in good hands comes right at the start. One of the script’s earliest character introductions is—of all people—Peter Lorre. In this world, he’s a scientist at the Acme Corporation (not to be confused with the grocery chain) evading security guards with a variety of nefarious devices like Expanding Boulders and Large Magnets. The second sign of quality is the law firm handling the titular court case: Avery, Jones, and Maltese. It’s the kind of naming convention that could only come from a creative team with a deep reverence not just for the Looney Tunes, but the medium of animation itself. – Devan S. ( full review )

Where to Stream: VOD

The Currents (Milagros Mumenthaler)

Writer-director Milagros Mumenthaler paints an intimate portrait of a woman trying to reckon with her fractured identity, trying not to fall into the grip of madness. Mumenthaler understands that motherhood requires an element of performance that reminds the mother that her life is no longer hers alone. Though the love for her daughter is still there inside, she cowers from it, preoccupied with inspecting the current shape of her life. In therapy, Lina expresses a fear of water’s power and the strength of a current that could wash her away. It’s as if she now knows the fragility of her existence, and that the confidence that once governed her was washed away when she jumped off the bridge. Despite the eccentricity of her fears, the emotions behind them are painfully relatable to any woman who feels that the inertia of her life has taken over. – Jourdain S. ( full review )

Where to Stream: Kino Film Collection , VOD

Disclosure Day (Steven Spielberg)

Certain beliefs unite all of humanity. Take, for example, the idea that the extraordinary is possible. Or, even more, that the impossible is possible. Steven Spielberg isn’t shy about believing in extraterrestrial life, and he doesn’t think you should be either. He’s so sincere about this aloof-yet-sky-high-stakes concept that he’s returning to it again with a very simple profundity in tow: “Empathy is the core of animate existence–our evolutionary advantage.” And he intends to remind us of our capacity for such. – Luke H. ( full review )

Where to Stream: Peacock , VOD

Dry Leaf (Alexandre Koberidze)

Languorous without becoming laborious, meditative without becoming meandering, abstract without becoming abstruse, Alexandre Koberidze’s Dry Leaf is a road movie unlike any other. It follows Irakli (David Koberidze), a father in search of his daughter, a sports photographer whose sudden disappearance is less of an enigma to solve than a vehicle for Koberidze’s imagination to serenely drift. Featuring Giorgi Koberidze’s charming, addictive score and shot on a Sony Ericsson, the fuzzy look of which transforms mundane landscapes into foreign-seeming textural images and hypnotic sequences, Dry Leaf , at 186 minutes, actively heightens our perception to its bucolic territory, its singular wavelength. It’s the kind of film where the destination is less important than the journey, where submission to its logic is more meaningful than a resistance, and where, like a vivid dream, its numinous sensations linger long after viewing. No matter the resolution, Koberidze has established himself as a modern enchanter. – Nirris N.

Where to Stream: MUBI

EPiC: Elvis Presley in Concert (Baz Luhrmann)

In a way, EPiC is the most naturalistic film Luhrmann’s ever made, unconventionally employing the traditional layout of a tell-all music doc. But that’s a misnomer under the singular, kinetic eye of the Moulin Rouge and Romeo + Juliet director, who brings a dazzling energy—as show-stopping in cinematic terms as The King’s concerts were in the musical—to the well-worn documentary style that electrifies the viewer into a state of ecstasy from start to finish. – Luke H. ( full review )

Where to Stream: Paramount+ , VOD

The Fence (Claire Denis)

Claire Denis’ The Fence is perhaps not so evocative and penetrating as her career high marks, but it’s stuck with me far more than most of the past year’s most “acclaimed” films. Ethan Vestby said in his review , “Is the idea of a Claire Denis film changing? There was likely an image one formed in their head when that name emerged: elliptical, sexy, avant-garde. Yet recent works are suggesting a different direction, one far more direct and less mysterious. It can even be said that her newest, The Fence , plays like a final film––not necessarily as a grand summation or statement, but like a stripping-down of almost everything possible.”

Where to Stream: AMC+ , VOD

Fiume o morte! (Igor Bezinović)

Learning about Gabriele D’Annunzio’s 16-month occupation of Fiume, a tale vividly retold in Igor Bezinović’s new, Tiger Award-winning documentary Fiume o Morte! , I spared a thought for Yukio Mishima. D’Annunzio’s life didn’t end so theatrically, but the two men––celebrated writers and hyper-nationalists with hubristic military dreams and similarly contested legacies––certainly shared a taste for the quixotic and chaotic. Was D’Annunzio a fascist colonizer, as those who still remember him in Fiume (now Rijeka, Croatia) claim, or was he the admirable dreamer as romantic as his poems? A century later, the jury’s still out. – Rory O. ( full review )

Where to Stream: VOD

The Invite (Olivia Wilde)

Small in scale, yet so much greater than the sum of its parts, Wilde conducts her quartet of players to an orchestral performance. She builds the dramatic tension of a relationship-turned-powder-keg from years of complacency and poor communication over staccato strings until it reaches its summit, only for it to drop and rise again. Employing just four principal actors, including herself, and a single apartment, it’s an impressive feat to pull off and a testament to her progression as actor-turned-director. – Kent M. W. ( full review )

Where to Stream: HBO Max (starting Friday) , VOD

Is God Is (Aleshea Harris)

“Complicated” doesn’t begin to describe the family history that twin sisters Racine (Kara Young) and Anaia (Mallori Johnson) are facing in Is God Is , Aleshea Harris’ film adaptation of her acclaimed play. A directorial debut brimming with storytelling ingenuity and stylistic verve, the revenge tale follows the sisters on their path toward justice after their father left them and their mother for dead. While sometimes the theatrics at play can take away from the desired emotional connection, it’s quite an impressive first outing in the directorial chair for Harris, hopefully leading to more opportunities. – Jordan R.

Where to Stream: Prime Video, VOD

The Last One for the Road (Francesco Sossai)

It doesn’t take long to work out where you are in The Last One for the Road ––for the backroads of Veneto, Italy, Francesco Sossai’s delightful new movie has the unmistakable specificity of a life spent there. What you instead start to wonder is the when of it all. The protagonists are a pair of rogues in their 50s––one of whom, Doriano (Pierpaolo Capovilla), wears a shirt the color of a tobacco stain, the other, Carlobianchi (Sergio Romano), a style of bushy mustache I’ve rarely seen onscreen since Bruno Ganz sported a similar one in The American Friend. Only after stumbling into a group of Gen Z students––the most visible dressed in the headgear of an Egyptian goddess––late at night along a Venice canal do we realize that our heroes exist in the here and now. If it wasn’t for their innate knack for catching last orders, regardless of the watering hole, you’d almost call them men out of time. – Rory O. ( full review)

Where to Stream: The Criterion Channel , VOD

Maddie’s Secret (John Early)

You can’t accuse John Early of not committing. Through the majority of his acting career, the comedian has become a reliable avatar for a palpable, toxic, hilarious narcissism, playing characters oblivious to the world outside the bubbles they’ve so thoroughly cultivated. That was particularly evident over four seasons of Search Party , as well as last year’s Stress Positions , a Sundance favorite that exposed the absurdity of living in quarantine over a masked summer. As an agoraphobic tenant in a Brooklyn brownstone, Early took the situation’s disaster and approached it through his very specific kind of self-assured, righteous mania to such an extent that his freak-outs are still rattling around in my brain. – Jake K-S. ( full review )

Where to Stream: VOD

Miroirs No. 3 (Christian Petzold)

One of the greatest directors working today, Christian Petzold returned this year with another masterfully enigmatic, gripping drama. Luke Hicks said in his Cannes review , “ Miroirs No. 3 is the kind of work best-served with as little information as possible. It’s not among Petzold’s greatest, but films like Barbara and Undine have made that a very high bar to clear. It’s textbook Petzold, which I mean as a major compliment. Don’t expect all of the mysteries to be uncovered. There is no big explainer moment or narratively satisfying closure, the likes of which Petzold rejects, but the enigmas that do reveal themselves yield rare treasures.”

Where to Stream: MUBI , VOD

Night Nurse (Georgia Bernstein)

We know so little about the life of Eleni (Cemre Paksoy), a nurse working in an upscale retirement community, until something awakens in her. Directed by Georgia Bernstein, the perverse Night Nurse doesn’t quite qualify as a psychosexual thriller, despite underlying erotic tension; there is something more seductive and sinister under the surface. – John F. ( full review )

Where to Stream: AMC+ , VOD

Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie (Matt Johnson)

The funniest, most unpredictable, “no, seriously, how the fuck did they do that???” movie of the year is about two guys, an RV, and a dream to play the Rivoli. Matt Johnson and Jay McCarroll’s big screen take on their cult-classic web (and later cable) series is perfectly legible for newbies, throwing off enough gags across the spectrum that something will land, be it a particular movie seen in a theater to a stray comment from a passerby. As much a triumph of low-budget/mockumentary filmmaking as it is one of sheer audacity, it simply must be seen to be believed. – Devan S. ( full review )

Where to Stream: Hulu , VOD

Our Land (Nuestra Tierra) (Lucrecia Martel)

There is a direct and conscious through-line between Lucrecia Martel’s previous historical film Zama to her contemporary legal documentary Nuestra Tierra . We see the lives of indigenous communities in Argentina continue to be treated with little regard and a clear class and racial fissure exists in the nation. Martel films the court scenes and the footage of the disputed land as two battlegrounds spanning time. The murder of the Chuchagasta indigenous community leader Javie Chocobar at the hands of corrupt businessmen and bureaucrats reflects and mirrors the history of Argentina as, to this day, a disputed territory. While Martel’s cinema is known for its heavy use of metaphor, blending of fantasy and realism with impressionistic camerawork, this is a movie that pares everything down to cinema’s base elements, making crystal clear what is at stake. – Soham G.

Where to Stream: The Criterion Channel , VOD

Remake (Ross McElwee)

Though best-known for his landmark reflexive documentary Sherman’s March , Ross McElwee crafted his most aching, personal film yet with Remake , one of the very best films of 2026. Partially structured around McElwee’s process when a company hopes to adapt Sherman’s March (a new restoration of which also comes to digital this week ), its true nature soon reveals itself: a tribute to the director’s son and self-reckoning as McElwee ponders his hand in his progeny’s path. It’s a nakedly confessional, deeply emotional work that will break any parent’s heart into a million pieces.

Where to Stream: VOD

The Rivals of Amziah King (Andrew Patterson)

Like the Church potluck to which Amziah King introduces his one-time foster daughter Kateri, The Rivals of Amziah King is a gleeful mashup of genres and tones blending bluegrass music, comedy, revenge, and heist-thriller elements into a tasty homestyle buffet full of eccentric characters and thick Southern accents. It’s a strong follow-up to the promise Andrew Patterson displayed in his resourceful debut feature The Vast of Night ––even when this mash-up seems a little uneven and indulgent, with a heavy use of formal techniques, from slow-motion to ironic music. – John F. ( full review )

Where to Stream: VOD

Romería (Carla Simón)

Continuing in the low-key register of her Golden Bear winner Alcarràs , Carla Simón returns with Romería , another tale of intergenerational dissonance. A film about the stories families choose to tell and the ones they bury deep inside, it unfurls on Spain’s Atlantic coast, where 18-year-old orphan Marina (Llúcia Garcia) hopes to reunite with her paternal family. It’s also a story about displacement and yearning for lost roots, themes that cut close to the bone for a director whose parents died of AIDS when she was still a child, and who reunited with her father’s family in the town of Vigo, Galicia, where the film is set, at the same age. Simón has always been an autobiographical filmmaker; Romería might be her most personal work yet. – Rory O. ( full review )

Where to Stream: The Criterion Channel , VOD

Rose of Nevada (Mark Jenkin)

The films of Mark Jenkin ooze a hypnotic, seasick sensibility; to watch them is to be lulled by their restless jumps through time and space, their ability to convert his home turf of Cornwall into a suspended world where facts and visions collide in stupefying dioramas. The director is a spinner of wandering tales, never fueled by linear plots so much as ambient forces: a ticking clock, gusts of wind, the distant roaring of waves. His dramas tend to pull your gaze from people and toward the inanimate objects that litter their surroundings. It’s here––in the interstice between the fictional foreground and non-fictional background––that the actual story often lies. – Leonardo G. ( full review )

Where to Stream: MUBI , VOD

Serpent’s Path (Kiyoshi Kurosawa)

Transplanting the action from Tokyo to Paris, the new Serpent’s Path is fairly faithful to its predecessor in terms of story beats. Albert (Damien Bonnard) joins forces with Japanese psychiatrist Sayoko (Ko Shibasaki), with the latter being a gender-flipped interpretation of the previous schoolteacher role. The film kicks off with them abducting Laval (a brilliant weasel of a performance from Mathieu Amalric), a low-level accountant for the company Minard, whose employees are secretly involved in a child-trafficking organization known as The Circle. Laval’s interrogation takes place in the kind of decrepit, abandoned warehouse we’ve seen in much of Kurosawa’s work, and with the aid of deeper shadows and sharper framing from cinematographer Alexis Kavyrchine (who worked with the director on his previous French-language feature, Daguerrotype ), the palpable sense of terror is turned up further from the very beginning. Serpent’s Path is the type of film that makes you want a shower afterwards, the hours spent in the muck of this environment and the psychology of these characters taking a toll on your spirit. – Mitchell B. ( full review )

Where to Stream: The Criterion Channel , VOD

Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma (Jane Schoenbrun)

Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow follow-up Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma is a wildly entertaining exploration of the slasher film, erotic pleasure, and everything in between. Led by Hannah Einbinder and Gillian Anderson, Rory O’Connor said in his Critic’s Pick review from Cannes , “Shot masterfully by their regular cinematographer Eric Yue (Alex G also makes a welcome return as composer), the movie-within-the-movie’s formative kill scene is so mesmerizing that you’ll welcome Schoenbrun’s decision to play it again and again––all the better to get a feel for how Kris’ obsessions have led them to the movie’s climax, and perhaps their own. Yue and Schoenbrun’s approaches also perfectly align when capturing actresses’ faces, often in achingly beautiful close-ups that only occasionally allow for a flicker of menace. ‘There’s a hole at the bottom of the lake,’ Billy explains to Kris in one of those moments, setting off a sequence that is quickly becoming Schoenbrun’s signature—that churning sense of movie spiraling a drain as it drags you down with it.”

Where to Stream: MUBI , VOD

Two Pianos (Arnaud Desplechin)

The past rears its not-so-ugly head in Two Pianos , Arnaud Desplechin’s latest film exploring the ways gorgeous people make an even bigger mess out of the messiness of life itself. Set amidst the world of classical music in Lyon, this tale of a tortured pianist’s reunion with his also-tortured first love contains the literary and melodramatic elements one normally expects from Desplechin, who––having not received a theatrical release since 2017’s Ismael’s Ghosts ––has fallen out of favor in the U.S. Fortunately that’s not the case in his home country, where he’s maintained a prolific output that continues attracting some of France’s top actors. With Two Pianos he’s put together a rich, thoughtful look at how we can shape our lives around our biggest regrets. – C.J. P. ( full review )

Where to Stream: Kino Film Collection , VOD

A Useful Ghost (Ratchapoom Boonbunchachoke)

While ghosts and spirits have long been the conduit for cinematic scares and jolts, from The Innocents to Poltergeist to The Ring , a relatively recent wave of films exploring the supernatural has been more concerned with the tangible, emotional effects these specters can have on the living. In that sense, a spiritual cousin to the likes of Uncle Boonmee , Personal Shopper , A Ghost Story , and Light from Light , Ratchapoom Boonbunchachoke’s directorial debut A Useful Ghost is a strange, tranquil, humorous exploration of the conundrums that would emerge were ghosts an accepted occurrence in everyday life, and what such phantoms could illuminate about the social and political troubles of modern Thailand and industrialization at large. – Jordan R. ( full review )

Where to Stream: Prime Video, VOD

Yes (Nadav Lapid)

Tel Aviv native, defector, and auteur Nadav Lapid opens his fifth feature in a catastrophic state of carouse. A filmmaker known for his employment of trademark dance sequences, Lapid is back with an equally visceral but uncharacteristically clubby groove in Yes , a work whose sarcastically enthusiastic title points to the relentless ridicule and hometown mockery that defines it. – Luke H. ( full review )

Where to Stream: Kino Film Collection , VOD

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "走入摄影师安德斯·彼得森（Anders Petersen）的世界，在里窝那（Livorno）体验为期5天的变革性街头摄影之旅。在这些高强度的日子里，你将拍摄交织着人类情感的复杂氛围。从威尼斯新城（Venezia Nuova）的历史小巷到熙熙攘攘的工作港口，里窝那将成为你的画布，挑战你的感知并打磨你的个人声音。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们会谈论摄影、电影、生活、爱……这就是安德斯的世界！我们将拍摄全新的照片，为日后继续开展的新项目寻找灵感。我们的想象力——以及安德斯那层出不穷的创造力——将带我们去往何方，我们就去往何方。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "期待你的视角发生转变。这一周当然是关于摄影的，但它主要关乎你自己。它关乎你如何想要使用相机，来重新诠释你内心与外在的世界。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这一周的时间将分配给理论课、拍摄时间、讨论以及分享时刻。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "通常我们在早晨上理论课，首先审阅你的作品集，然后对在拍摄现场产出的作品进行集体评图。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这不只是一场工作坊——这是一次深入原始人类连接、叙事深度与观看艺术的高强度之旅。在安德斯·彼得森标志性的氛围与亲密感方法的引导下，你将突破自己技艺的边界，探索里窝那粗粝的港口、历史街区和野性十足的本土生活。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "自2006年我们初次相遇并开始他在托斯卡纳的工作坊教学以来，安德斯·彼得森就一直是TPW的“常客”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在那里度过了许多年后，我们决定继续我们共同的行旅项目，探索意大利不同的城市。当时我们并不知道，但我们已经开启了一个项目，带领我们探索了意大利的许多城市：威尼斯、罗马、锡拉库萨、巴勒莫、那不勒斯、博洛尼亚、热那亚、佛罗伦萨，以及最近的巴里和都灵", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们2027年的目的地将是位于托斯卡纳的里窝那，它位于佛罗伦萨西南方80分钟车程处。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "意大利 里窝那", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "2027年4月24-30日", "translated": true}]
