article_text:
Step into the world of photographer Anders Petersen for a transformative 5-day street photography experience in Livorno.Over these intensive days, you will photograph a mixed atmosphere of human emotion. From the historic alleys of Venezia Nuova to the bustling working port, Livorno will serve as your canvas to challenge your perception and refine your personal voice.

We will talk about photography, cinema, life, love… it’s Anders’ world! We will take new photographs, find inspiration for new projects to carry on later. We will go wherever our imaginations – and Anders’ ceaseless creativity – takes us.

Expect your perspectives to shift. The week will be about photography, of course, but it will be mainly about you. It will be about how you want to use your camera to re-interpret the world, within and without you.

The week will be divided between theory classes, shooting time, discussion, sharing moments.

Usually we run theory classes in the morning, looking at your portfolio first and then having a group critique of the work produced on location.

This isn’t just a workshop—it’s an intensive journey into raw human connection, narrative depth, and the art of seeing. Guided by Anders Petersen’s iconic approach to atmosphere and intimacy, you will push the boundaries of your craft, exploring Livorno’s gritty harbors, historic quarters, and untamed local life.

Anders Petersen has been a “regular” at TPW since 2006, when we first met and he started teaching at our workshops in Tuscany.

After many years there, we decided to continue our project together on the road, exploring different cities in Italy. We did not know by then, but we were starting a project that took us to explore many cities of Italy: Venice, Rome, Siracusa, Palermo, Naples, Bologna, Genoa, Florence and recently Bari and Torino

Our destination for 2027 will be Livorno in Tuscany, 80 minutes south-west of Florence.

Livorno, Italy

April 24-30, 2027

article_text:
Japanese filmmaker Ishikawa Hiroshi , whose credits include “Tokyo.sora,” “Su-ki-da.” and “Petal Dance,” is back with his first feature in 13 years. His new film, “ the blue we touch ” (original title: “Awo no Jo”), is in post-production and will be released in Japan in 2027 by Bitters End, which unveiled the project ahead of the Tokyo International Film Festival ‘s TIFFCOM market.

The ensemble drama centers on a pair of former friends and traces the hard-to-name feelings that pass between people. Nao heads the cast as Mitsu, 29, who does contract web design and wants a permanent job, along with a chance to make work that connects with an audience. She is drawn to Fujino (Nakajima Ayumu), who runs HR at her firm, and slowly starts to share grievances she has kept quiet about for a long time.

Related Stories

Nicolas Cage Says He’s ‘Probably Not’ Working With Amazon Again After Refusing to Sign AI Waiver for ‘Spider-Noir,' Teases Joining 'True Detective'

'Amanda the Adventurer' Video Game Movie Adaptation in the Works From Blumhouse, MatPat and Epic Pictures

Karata Erika plays Ayane, who works nights while preparing for a career as a public prosecutor. She crosses paths with Tomoki (Aoki Yuzu), an art student who can’t get his figure drawing right, and agrees to sit for him as a model. The arrangement opens up Tomoki’s work, while Ayane finds her way back to memories she treasures.

Nakano Arisa, who made her screen debut in Wim Wenders’ “Perfect Days,” plays Nozomi, a classmate of Tomoki’s who watches him change up close.

Ishikawa handled writing, directing and editing duties. He won awards as a commercials director before moving into features with “Tokyo.sora” in 2002. “Su-ki-da.” followed in 2006 and earned him best director at the New Montreal FilmFest, with “Petal Dance” arriving in 2013. His work is known for its careful handling of color and its feel for the mood of ordinary days.

Nao’s earlier films include “The Last 10 Years” and “Sensei’s Pious Lie.” Karata has appeared in “Asako I & II,” “Desert of Namibia” and Netflix’s “The Queen of Villains,” while Nakajima’s credits span TBS’ “Until the T-Shirt Dries,” “Happyend” and “Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy.” Aoki’s résumé includes “5 Centimeters per Second,” “Blue Lock” and “Minamata.”

Bitters End has been active for more than three decades, releasing films in Japan by Hamaguchi Ryusuke, Bong Joon-ho, the Dardenne brothers, Jia Zhangke, Roy Andersson and Gianfranco Rosi. Its recent releases include “Below the Clouds,” “Young Mothers” and “The Odyssey.”

On the production side, the company’s credits include Oscar winner “Drive My Car” and Locarno Golden Leopard recipient “Two Seasons, Two Strangers.” This year, “All of a Sudden,” which took a prize at Cannes and is Japan’s Oscar submission for international feature, played in competition, and “All the Lovers in the Night” made the Un Certain Regard lineup.

Bitters End is now growing its international sales operation. “In My Father’s Room” competed at San Sebastián, where it took the Fipresci Prize and the Ateneo Guipuzcoano Award.

article_text:
Sponsored

Asia NOW Returns to Paris for its 12th Edition

Asia NOW returns to Paris for its 12th edition from October 20 to 24, 2026, at the Monnaie de Paris, showcasing the incredible talents of over 50 galleries and 150 artists. This year’s theme, “Sentimental Value,” invites us to reflect on how artworks acquire meaning through memory, relationships, and connections, with a poignant focus on soil as a symbol of grounding.

Participating galleries include Esther Schipper, Sabrina Amrani, Kaikai Kiki Gallery, The Drawing Room, and many more, presenting a dynamic range of solo, duo, and group exhibitions. Special projects will inspire awe, including Vessels of Memory by Jogja Biennale, curated by Alia Swastika. Spanning painting, weaving, soil, sound, performance, and archival practices, the project features Citra Sasmita, Ines Katamso, Hashel El Lamki, Timoteus Anggawan Kusno, Jumaadi, Nathalie Muchamad, Dicky Takndare, and Rani Jambak. Further highlights include a captivating presentation of the Saudi art scene by Villa Hegra and a project by Kalhath Foundation celebrating the beauty of Indian craftsmanship.

Adding another dimension to the programme, Punk Orientalism Studio, founded by Dr. Sara Raza, Artistic Director and Chief Curator of the Center for Contemporary Art Tashkent, presents I Open My Mouth and Speak Art , a week-long programme of conversations, presentations, readings, and performances exploring art, language, migration, cultural memory, and resistance.

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Black Bear CEO Teddy Schwarzman has seen some ups and downs in the transition from financier-producer-foreign-sales-company-UK-distributor to full-on North American distribution company Black Bear Pictures. The Blackstone scion is smart and experienced enough to know the risks inherent in competing in the fraught indie marketplace. But even in the face of frosty reviews for “Christy,” starring Sydney Sweeney with her bosom buried from view in a boxing movie, he mounted a full-on theatrical release and demonstrated his support for the filmmakers and would-be Oscar contender.", "links": [{"text": "Black Bear", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/black-bear/"}, {"text": "Teddy Schwarzman", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/teddy-schwarzman/"}, {"text": "Blackstone scion", "url": "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_A._Schwarzman"}, {"text": "“Christy,”", "url": "https://www.metacritic.com/movie/christy/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That didn’t happen. The $15-million movie grossed just under $2 million domestic. A year later, Schwarzman is soldiering on, having rejiggered his 65-person staff and executive team (CAA import Ben Kramer left earlier this year ) and betting on a range of indie films from critics’ faves “The Rivals of Amziah King” (which died at the box office) and “Tuner” ($14.6 million worldwide) to the Jason Statham survival adventure “Shelter” ($56 million worldwide), Jake Gyllenhaal action thriller “In the Grey” ($28.4 million worldwide) and “Spa Weekend” ($13.9 million worldwide).", "links": [{"text": "left earlier this year", "url": "https://deadline.com/2026/10/ben-kramer-black-bear-head-of-us-distribution-exiting-1237145475/"}, {"text": "“The Rivals of Amziah King”", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/movies/the-rivals-of-amziah-king-review-matthew-mcconaughey-1235102696/"}, {"text": "“Tuner”", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/features/interviews/tuner-director-daniel-roher-interview-1235196018/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RP_B2706.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "Arash Ashtiani, Pegah Ahangarani and Brent Lang at IndieWire Art of the Doc 2026 held at Lumen on October 19, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/202605733_1_RWD_1920.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "Who Killed Alex Odeh?", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This weekend Black Bear is releasing Sundance breakout “ Wicker ” in 1,400 theaters, where it is expected to open to $6 to $8 million. The medieval-period romance showcases British star Olivia Colman as a spinster fishmonger who commissions a wicker husband ( Alexander Skarsgard ). He wildly exceeds her romantic fantasies, breaks her bed, and upends every marriage in the village.", "links": [{"text": "Sundance breakout", "url": "https://www.metacritic.com/movie/wicker/"}, {"text": "Wicker", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/wicker/"}, {"text": "Olivia Colman", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/olivia-colman/"}, {"text": "Alexander Skarsgard", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/alexander-skarsgard-2/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Black Bear joined the project at the script stage as international sales agent, partnering with financiers Topic and Tango. When Black Bear finally saw how the film played at Sundance, they acquired North American distribution rights. “What we’ve always tried to do with Black Bear,” said Schwarzman on Zoom, “is find films that are original, or stand out in their genre, have a real vision from a director standpoint, and make you feel in some way. … We couldn’t find a more original film than ‘Wicker,’ despite the fact that it’s an adapted short story, but the entire conceit was executed near perfection. … We were blown away that there was something weird and provocative and horny and sexual and ultimately actually incredibly emotional and human.”", "links": [{"text": "film", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/film/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Black Bear has also hired a new marketing team, scooping up former Neon executive Bianca Parkes, a graphics whiz who knows strategy, guerilla marketing, print campaigns, and merchandising, after her husband Christian left to found Clockwork at Warner Bros. , as well as PR vet Heather Phillips, who has worked all sides of the studio/indie street. article_text:
Black Bear CEO Teddy Schwarzman has seen some ups and downs in the transition from financier-producer-foreign-sales-company-UK-distributor to full-on North American distribution company Black Bear Pictures. The Blackstone scion is smart and experienced enough to know the risks inherent in competing in the fraught indie marketplace. But even in the face of frosty reviews for “Christy,” starring Sydney Sweeney with her bosom buried from view in a boxing movie, he mounted a full-on theatrical release and demonstrated his support for the filmmakers and would-be Oscar contender.

That didn’t happen. The $15-million movie grossed just under $2 million domestic. A year later, Schwarzman is soldiering on, having rejiggered his 65-person staff and executive team (CAA import Ben Kramer left earlier this year ) and betting on a range of indie films from critics’ faves “The Rivals of Amziah King” (which died at the box office) and “Tuner” ($14.6 million worldwide) to the Jason Statham survival adventure “Shelter” ($56 million worldwide), Jake Gyllenhaal action thriller “In the Grey” ($28.4 million worldwide) and “Spa Weekend” ($13.9 million worldwide).

This weekend Black Bear is releasing Sundance breakout “ Wicker ” in 1,400 theaters, where it is expected to open to $6 to $8 million. The medieval-period romance showcases British star Olivia Colman as a spinster fishmonger who commissions a wicker husband ( Alexander Skarsgard ). He wildly exceeds her romantic fantasies, breaks her bed, and upends every marriage in the village.

Black Bear joined the project at the script stage as international sales agent, partnering with financiers Topic and Tango. When Black Bear finally saw how the film played at Sundance, they acquired North American distribution rights. “What we’ve always tried to do with Black Bear,” said Schwarzman on Zoom, “is find films that are original, or stand out in their genre, have a real vision from a director standpoint, and make you feel in some way. … We couldn’t find a more original film than ‘Wicker,’ despite the fact that it’s an adapted short story, but the entire conceit was executed near perfection. … We were blown away that there was something weird and provocative and horny and sexual and ultimately actually incredibly emotional and human.”

Black Bear has also hired a new marketing team, scooping up former Neon executive Bianca Parkes, a graphics whiz who knows strategy, guerilla marketing, print campaigns, and merchandising, after her husband Christian left to found Clockwork at Warner Bros. , as well as PR vet Heather Phillips, who has worked all sides of the studio/indie street. The “Wicker” marketing has been inspired, from a 6 foot 6 wicker standee to the “dream boyfriend” campaign.

Leaning into the weird side of this romantic fantasy, the “Wicker” trailer went viral across Black Bear’s owned channels, generating 80.3 million views in its first two weeks, with 70.5 million of those views coming organically (nearly 88 percent), generating social media conversations far and wide. On TikTok alone, trailer-related reactions and user-generated content amassed an additional 322 million views, bringing the combined total to over 402 million views. Needless to say, this evidence of consumer interest boosted the distributor’s confidence in the film’s commerciality.

The rap on Black Bear, which they deny, is that they don’t spend. Schwarzman is considered to be frugal. But they are spending now. They learned from watching Netflix’s handling of another Sundance hit, “Train Dreams,” which relaunched with a fresh campaign at the fall festivals with strong results.

Thus “Wicker” played a selection of fall festivals, skipping Toronto but selling out instantly at Middleburg. On the awards front “The Favourite” Oscar-winner Colman (boasting new hair extensions imitated on the red carpet by the ingenious Skarsgard) is in the Actress conversation as well as the hair and makeup team.

Schwarzman has figured out his ongoing strategy, he said, “We are now having a true north of the type of movies that we want to be making and that we want to be releasing, which are filmmaker-centric, original, entertaining, and with some substance to what they are.”

In today’s trying times, it may be that a sexy escapist fantasy is just what audiences need.
excerpt_original: It's a year since CEO Teddy Schwarzman embraced North American distribution with “Christy.” What has he learned?

Foto: Sander van Wettum.", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "2021年5月。正值首次封锁期间。我在网上观看了一场研讨会，其中以赛亚·洛佩斯（Isaiah Lopez）与阿德奥拉·阿德雷米（Adeola Aderemi）就同性恋社群内部的结构性种族主义展开对话。某个时刻，阿德奥拉说出了一句让我铭记于心的话：", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Our archives are our activism. — Adeola Aderemi", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/LR_W139_Thenatureofremembering_2026_photo_by_sandervanwettum-12-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Komtouch Napattaloong – Lady White Blood: Excerpts (2026); Kaisa Saarinen, Field Notes pt. 1 (2026); Bart Seng Wen Long, Field Interviews #3 & #4 (2026), The Nature of Remembering, W139. Foto: Sander van Wettum.", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/5_TNOR_promo_KomtouchNapattaloong-1024x768.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Bart Seng Wen Long – still from Field Interview #3 (2026).", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "12 januari 2023", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在比利时，一名有色人种女性苏鲁尔·阿布达（Sourour Abouda）在呼救被忽视后，死于警察局拘留室。她是两年来在比利时监狱中于神秘情况下死亡的第三名有色人种。她的死最初被警方伪装成自杀。这起案件以及它所暴露的结构性不公深深触动了我。一颗种子就此播下。这颗种子后来成为了“日出纪念碑”（Sunrise Monument）：一座以巨石阵为基础的虚拟纪念碑；它在日出时分朝着冬至/夏至方向建造，那是变化与转化的时刻。它成为了一个地方，我们可以在那里将成为警察暴力受害者的有色人种的名字建档归档。这是一个拒绝让他们在统计数据中消失、并将统计数据剥夺之物归还给他们的场所：他们的名字、他们的А性、他们的记忆。在我后来创作的表演《Plum Road Tea Dream_The Performance》中，我们大声念出了他们的名字。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "2025年2月。我前往鹿特丹，在伊赛亚（Isiah）指导的一个工作坊中遇到了他们：Black Visual Grammar Edition V: Roots & Robots — Science & Technology。这是一场专为 BIPOC（黑人、原住民及有色人种）人群举办的聚会，大家一起制作拼贴画，同时分享空间、对话与食物。我制作了一幅拼贴画，后来将其命名为《The Black Mage’s Wand》。我在那里还遇到了拉维尔（Lawil）。她拓宽了媒介的边界。她的拼贴画几乎变成了一座雕塑：纸张被立体化运用，不再甘于停留在平面表面。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/LR_W139_Thenatureofremembering_2026_photo_by_sandervanwettum-9-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Michèle Boulogne – Mining the Sky (2020, 2026), The Nature of Remembering, W139. Foto: Sander van Wettum.", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/LR_W139_Thenatureofremembering_2026_photo_by_sandervanwettum-3-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Laura Fong Prosper and Tin Wilke –\nMemorial Matter (2023), The Nature of Remembering, W139. Foto: Sander van Wettum.", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "2026年3月13日。亲爱的塞缪尔·拜杜：我叫拉维尔·卡拉马（Lawil Karama），是一名居住在荷兰的艺术家。我与策展人梅根·霍特格（Megan Hoetger）一同写信，邀请您为阿姆斯特丹 W139 艺术空间即将举办的群展《The Nature of Remembering》（……）做出贡献。（……）我们发现您最近的表演作品《Plum Road Tea Dream_The Performance》在对待技术之仪式化运用、身份认同问题以及对预期性悲伤（anticipatory grief）的处理方式上，其真实态度令人难以置信地感人。我读着这封邀请函。有时，只有当你回首时，前路才会显现。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "2026年4月4日。当拉维尔和梅根在我们于安特卫普重新排演该表演时走进来，我禁不住微笑。我们此时已经进行了一次 Zoom 会议，并交换了电子邮件。拉维尔向我讲述了她将在 W139 展出的作品：试图重构乌干达姆巴莱（Mbale）在1973年2月10日的天空——那是伊迪·阿明（Idi Amin）政权下公开处决发生的时间与地点。我想象着天空作为一个实体，见证了这些受害者的死亡。接着，我想到了我自己的哀悼仪式。想到了“日出纪念碑”。想到了被大声念出的名字。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "接受大气原本的样子：一种持续的、包罗万象的存在，它没有刻意记录任何东西，但其物理状态是可以被重构的。它环绕着这些事件，见证了它们，在其特定的气象条件下承载着躯体与暴力。——梅根·霍特格（Megan Hoetger）", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/1_TNOR_promo_LawilKarama-699x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Lawil Karama – Algorithm of Colour: Reflection Series – Sky 14:00 EAT, February 10, 1973 Mbale, Uganda (2026), KunstRAI X Rietveld Alumni 2026: paralelepípedo, picture by Lucia Del Valle Ramirez.", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/LR_W139_Thenatureofremembering_2026_photo_by_sandervanwettum-15-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Lawil Karama – Algorithm of Colour (2026), The Nature of Remembering, W139. Foto: Sander van Wettum.", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "2026年9月。我漫步于展览之中，花时间在每一件作品前驻足。无形的线索渐渐变得清晰。身体、历史、技术、风景和代际之间的线索。我看到了一群有色人种艺术家利用技术来描绘各种形式的哀悼。这种哀悼跨越代际与海洋，将我们与那些从未素面相识的人连接在一起。为殖民主义而哀悼，为过去以及尚未发生的未来而哀悼，从有色人种的躯体到太空中的矿物。为失去的土地以及对大地所孕育之物的持续滥用而哀悼。我渐渐开始明白，记忆并不必然意味着回望。它更像是一种环顾四周的方式。去感受空气中残留的东西。去倾听那些被强加沉默的事物。去寻找统计数据之下的名字，历史之下的躯体。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "或许，记忆也是一种为尚未发生之事做好准备的方式。我们不仅在为过去建档。我们还在寻找将它随身携带的方法。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/LR_W139_Thenatureofremembering_2026_photo_by_sandervanwettum-6-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "《The Nature of Remembering》，W139 艺术空间。摄影：桑德·范·韦特姆（Sander van Wettum）。", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/LR_W139_Thenatureofremembering_2026_photo_by_sandervanwettum-18-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "阿拉姆·李（Aram Lee）——《350,000 Leaks (Griefs)》（2024），《The Nature of Remembering》，W139。摄影：桑德·范·韦特姆（Sander van Wettum）。", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "—", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "2026年10月17日，塞缪尔将与《The Nature of Remembering》的创办艺术家拉维尔·卡拉马展开对话。您可以在此处找到更多信息。展览《The Nature of Remembering》将在 W13 展出至 11月1日止。", "links": [{"text": "Hier", "url": "https://w139.nl/event/plum-road-tea-dream_the-hangout/"}], "translated": true}]

article_text:
Samuel Baidoo verbindt in hun Plum Road Tea Dream gaming en trauma. Hen creëerde een game én voorstelling. Wie gaming associeert met escapisme en afzondering, stuit dankzij Plum Road Tea Dream op onverwachte lagen, waarin discriminatie en queerness een onvergetelijke vorm van troost vinden. Mister Motley vroeg Samuel te reflecteren op herinneren, naar aanleiding van de tentoonstelling The Nature of Remembering in W139, waar Plum Road Tea Dream onderdeel van is.

Een digitale plek om te rouwen, een game met helende krachten – over Plum Road Tea Dream van Samuel Baidoo

KAN NIET BESTAAT NIET: Samuel Baidoo

Mei 2021 Het is de eerste lockdown. Ik volg online een symposium waarin Isaiah Lopez met Adeola Aderemi in gesprek gaat over structureel racisme binnen de gay community. Op een bepaald moment spreekt Adeola een zin uit die bij me blijft:

Our archives are our activism. — Adeola Aderemi

12 januari 2023

In België sterft Sourour Abouda, een vrouw van kleur, in een politiecel nadat haar roep om hulp wordt genegeerd. Ze is de derde persoon van kleur die binnen twee jaar onder mysterieuze omstandigheden in een Belgische gevangenis overlijdt. Haar dood wordt aanvankelijk door de politie als zelfmoord voorgesteld. De zaak, en het structurele onrecht dat ze blootlegt, raakt me diep. Er wordt een zaadje geplant. Een zaadje voor wat later het Sunrise Monument zal worden: een virtueel monument gebaseerd op Stonehenge; gebouwd richting de zonsopgang tijdens een zonnewende, een moment van verandering en transformatie. Het werd een plek waar we de namen kunnen archiveren van mensen van kleur die slachtoffer werden van politiegeweld. Een plek die weigert hen te laten verdwijnen in statistieken en teruggeeft wat statistieken wegnemen: hun namen, hun menselijkheid, hun herinnering. In de voorstelling Plum Road Tea Dream_The Performance , die ik later maak, spreken we hun namen luidop.

Februari 2025 Ik reis naar Rotterdam en ontmoet Isiah tijdens een workshop die hen begeleidt: Black Visual Grammar Edition V: Roots & Robots — Science & Technology. Een bijeenkomst voor BIPOC-mensen om samen collages te maken, terwijl we ruimte, gesprekken en eten delen. Ik maak een collage die ik later The Black Mage’s Wand zal noemen. Ik ontmoet er ook Lawil. Zij duwt de grenzen van het medium open. Haar collage wordt bijna een sculptuur: papier wordt driedimensionaal gebruikt en weigert nog langer aan het oppervlak te blijven.

13 maart 2026 Dear Samuel Baidoo, My name is Lawil Karama, and I am an artist based in the Netherlands. Together with curator Megan Hoetger, I am writing to invite you to contribute to the upcoming group exhibition The Nature of Remembering (…) at W139, Amsterdam. (…) We found your recent performance piece Plum Road Tea Dream_The Performance to be incredibly moving in its authentic approach to the ritualistic use of technology, to questions of identity and processing anticipatory grief. Ik lees de uitnodiging. Soms wordt de weg pas zichtbaar wanneer je achteromkijkt.

4 april 2026 Ik kan een glimlach niet onderdrukken wanneer Lawil en Megan binnenkomen terwijl we de performance opnieuw spelen in Antwerpen. We hebben inmiddels een Zoom-gesprek gehad en e-mails uitgewisseld. Lawil vertelt over het werk dat zij in W139 zal tonen: een poging om de lucht boven Mbale, Oeganda, te reconstrueren op 10 februari 1973 – de dag en plaats van openbare executies onder het regime van Idi Amin. Ik denk aan de lucht als een entiteit die getuige is van de dood van deze slachtoffers. En vervolgens denk ik aan mijn eigen rouwritueel. Aan het Sunrise Monument . Aan namen die luidop worden uitgesproken.

To accept that the atmosphere simply is: a continuous, encompassing presence that records nothing deliberately, but whose physical state can be reconstructed. It surrounded the events, bore witness to them, held the bodies and the violence within its particular meteorological conditions. — Megan Hoetger

September 2026 Ik loop door de tentoonstelling, neem de tijd om bij elk werk stil te staan. Onzichtbare draden worden langzaam zichtbaar. Draden tussen lichamen, geschiedenissen, technologieën, landschappen en generaties. Ik zie een groep kunstenaars van kleur die technologie gebruiken om verschillende vormen van rouw in kaart te brengen. Rouw die ons, over generaties en oceanen heen, verbindt met mensen die we nooit persoonlijk hebben gekend. Rouw om kolonisatie, uit het verleden en dat wat nog moet komen, van de lichamen van mensen van kleur tot de mineralen van de ruimte. Rouw om verloren land en om het voortdurende misbruik van wat de aarde voortbrengt. En langzaam begin ik te begrijpen dat herinneren niet noodzakelijk betekent dat we achteromkijken. Het is eerder een manier om om ons heen te kijken. Te voelen wat in de lucht is achtergebleven. Te luisteren naar wat het zwijgen is opgelegd. De namen onder de statistieken te vinden, de lichamen onder de geschiedenissen.

Misschien is herinneren ook een manier om ons voor te bereiden op wat nog niet gebeurd is. We archiveren niet alleen het verleden. We zoeken manieren om het met ons mee te dragen.

—

Op 17 oktober 2026 gaat Samuel in dialoog met Lawil Karama, initiërend kunstenaar van The Nature of Remembering . Hier vind je meer informatie. De tentoonstelling The Nature of Remembering is nog tot en met 1 November te zien in W13.

article_text:
F or every reason except one, Once Upon a Time in Shaolin, the seventh album by the Wu-Tang Clan , should’ve been a commercial hit. The 31-track double album, recorded in secret between 2007 and 2013, reunited all of the remaining members of the hallowed Staten Island rap crew and featured eye-catching collaborators from the standard (Redman, offshoot group Wu-Tang Killa Bees) to the unexpected (Cher, Game of Thrones actor Carice van Houten). The sound, at least according to those involved, harkened back to the glory days of the group’s beginnings in the 90s.

But for years, almost no one heard it. The group only issued a single copy of Once Upon a Time in Shaolin – on CD, ensconced within layers of filigreed silver – with the stipulation, in legalese, that it could not be used for any commercial purposes for 88 years. The decree, either a stunt or a bold artistic statement on streaming’s devaluation of music, depending on your generosity and perhaps your net worth, succeeded in drumming up plenty of hype. And if you were anywhere around the blogosphere or cable news in 2015, you may recall that the beneficiary of that hype – the purchaser and thus single intended listener of this $2m musical treasure – was one Martin Shkreli , the “pharma bro” widely despised for gleefully hiking the costs of prescription drugs for profit.

A baseline level of fluency in these occasionally arcane events is assumed, if not required, for The Disciple: A Wu-Tang Fable, a new documentary which retraces the long saga of the buzzy single album, which still holds the record for the most valuable album ever sold, and its controversial producer. The film, directed by Joanna Natasegara (who won the best documentary short Oscar in 2016 for The White Helmets ) and executive produced by de facto Wu-Tang leader RZA, in fact goes much farther back than those covert recording sessions in the late 2000s; The Disciple, casual fans and Shkreli rubberneckers may be surprised to learn, is less a rehashing of the album’s infamy than a subjective, meandering examination of its controversial producer, Tarik Azzougarh, the Dutch Moroccan rapper and Wu-Tang associate also known as Cilvaringz.

Azzougarh, who narrates much of the film built around his personal archive (the Disciple doubles as an evolution of digital self-recording, from camcorders to selfies), can be a compelling lead: an unnervingly even-keeled presence, at once well-connected and under-the-radar, who came to the Clan via unrelenting ambition, having connected to their music with fellow immigrant friends, as outsiders in largely white Holland. But centering the bulk of a 105-minute film around one somewhat reticent lead can also prove repetitive and dead-ending, extraneous digressions on the Clan’s Hong Kong film references or tours around Staten Island notwithstanding.

Natasegara banks on, and draws out, Azzougarh’s fervent yet vaguely described obsession with Wu-Tang, particularly RZA, his eventual infiltration of their scene by phone and by simply showing up, his later entrenchment in RZA’s inner circle. There’s certainly something fascinating, at once hopeful and maybe sinister, in the ascendance of the self-described “fanboy” to the right-hand man. (See: last year’s underrated film Lurker .) But with minimal input from other Wu-Tang members beyond vague recollections and niceties, there’s little grist in what amounts to a slightly complicated and one-sided love letter to a genuinely formative, culture-shifting group. Though blessed by RZA, the leader only appears in archival footage or in ponderous grayscale interludes before a chess board, as if the relationship between mentor and subject were tricky and adversarial, not largely symbiotic.

Things pick up, at least, once the secret project gets going, bringing up artistic questions – why is a Warhol painting valued in the millions but not music? Why do people feel entitled to music for free? – and the practical matter of making one’s money back. Azzougarh’s idea to release but one CD, as the Mona Lisa of albums, was radical, but a multidimensional chess game this was not. As Cyrus Bozorgmehr, a seemingly bon vivant adviser to the album, recalls in the film, “buyers wanted to know what was hype, what was just a headline, what happened when you got to the nitty-gritty. And the answer was, we had no idea.”

Shkreli, for those wondering, doesn’t enter the story until the final third – the “poorest” of the potential buyers, one subject recalls, with a reported net worth of just $200m. There’s probably some intriguing nugget here for those locked into the story – that Shkreli planned to film a video threatening Wu-Tang members with mock guns, for one – but The Disciple is not trying to generate clickbait or conflict.

It does not, however, generate much interest, either. The film gestures at many potentially fruitful deep dives – on the passage of time and the curdling of one’s ambition, on the relationship between artist and fan, or just more simply the disputes over how to handle a true rogue like Shkreli – but largely does not wander, keeping viewers instead on the glossy surface or stranded in long-winded stories about parties. It’s unclear, for instance, where Azzougarh and RZA stand now, though one can probably assume that both endorse the exhibitions now being held by PleasrDao, an NFT collective, who bought the album for $4.75m in 2021. For true fans – the ones who’d, say, fly to Tasmania to hear the album or be thrilled by a 30-second snippet in a documentary – there’s plenty here to keep one’s attention. For everyone else, it remains a crazy headline.

The Disciple is out now in select US and UK cinemas and is streaming on Netflix

article_text:
A planned strike across all four Victoria and Albert Museum sites has been suspended as unionized staff return to the negotiating table following a new offer from management.

Members of Prospect and the Public and Commercial Services (PCS) union had voted to strike on October 29 and 30 amid a dispute over wages and working conditions. The dispute includes allegations that workers at the museum’s newest location, V&A East Storehouse, had fainted due to insufficient hydration breaks. The strike would have affected all four V&A sites: the flagship museum in South Kensington, the Young V&A children’s museum in East London, V&A East, and V&A East Storehouse.

The Guardian reports that the strike was suspended on Monday to allow time for talks with the Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service, following an “improved” offer from management.

“All V&A museums will be open this week, including all exhibitions, free displays and planned half-term activities. While we are working to reinstate as much of our public program as possible, unfortunately some events may still be cancelled or postponed – visitors are encouraged to check our website before traveling,” a V&A spokesperson told the Guardian .

The V&A unions are calling for a minimum 4 percent pay increase for workers earning above the living wage, time-and-a-half pay for work on bank holidays, and for the museum to become an accredited Real Living Wage employer, which would guarantee all staff an hourly wage that reflects London’s cost of living, currently estimated at £14.80 (about $20). They are also demanding improved conditions across the museum network, including more affordable dining options, shade in outdoor spaces when temperatures are forecast to reach 30°C (86°F) or higher, and better cooling in back-of-house areas. The union called a two-day strike in September.

V&A Storehouse, a publicly accessible museum storage facility in East London, has emerged as a flashpoint in the dispute. Its staff voted unanimously in July to strike, alleging that they are not given sufficient breaks to use the bathroom or drink water. Food and beverages, including sealed water bottles, are prohibited near the collection, according to a museum statement reiterating the policy. Staff, however, say the facility’s water fountains are regularly out of order and that they found beverage bottles in the collections hall the day after a private event.

The V&A has denied the union’s allegations about working conditions at the Storehouse and told ARTnews that management has been negotiating in good faith with the unions since February.

“We welcome this opportunity for constructive discussions with our trade union colleagues,” a museum spokesperson said in a statement. “Our latest pay offer delivers an average 4.18% pay rise and a 6.9% increase for our lowest-paid colleagues; increased bank holiday pay to 1.5, alongside a sector-leading bonus scheme and a subsidized food offer for staff at all V&A sites.”

I don’t know what’s next, but I have moved to a new, smaller studio near where I live in central Los Angeles. article_text:
Paul Mpagi Sepuya: Labyrinths & Ricochets

©Paul Mpagi Sepuya, Studio Diptych with Gazing Ball (_DSF5808, _DSF5811), 2024. Diptych, 19 x 24 inches each. From TRANCE

The orbit and arc of Paul Mpagi Sepuya ’s aesthetic trajectory has steadily tracked across my social media feeds over the last few years. For instance, Sepuya is the juror for this year’s La Jolla Athenaeum 34th Annual Juried Exhibition, which is near the university where he teaches in San Diego, California. He also lives in Los Angeles, where he is represented by Vielmetter Gallery . Known for his earlier bodies of work, Aperture describes the 2024 publication of Dark Room A-Z in the following ways: “Paul Mpagi Sepuya’s photography is grounded in a collaborative, rhizomatic approach to studio practice and portraiture. This volume unpacks his Dark Room series (2016–21), offering a deep dive into the thick network of references and the interconnected community of artists and subjects that Sepuya has interwoven throughout the images. The excavation and mapping of intellectual and artistic data points across the artist’s work is presented through […] a comprehensive cross-referencing of conceptual categories.”

Against the backdrop of his recent exhibition at the Sprengel Museum in Hanover, Germany, the second survey since his 2019 show (of 2006-2018 work) at the Contemporary Art Museum in St. Louis, Missouri, it seemed like a good time to ask the artist about his practice and how it dovetails with community.

Please tell us your name, where you are from, where you work, etc.

My name is Paul Mpagi Sepuya and I was born and grew up in San Bernardino, CA. Just east of Los Angeles. I lived in New York from 2000 to 2014, and then returned to Los Angeles, where I currently live and work. But I have a day job in La Jolla, where I’m a professor in the Visual Arts Department at UC San Diego. I just moved out of a studio building that I have been working in for the past ten years. This also is important because all of the work from the past decade in the related DARK ROOM projects has come to an end. I don’t know what’s next, but I have moved to a new, smaller studio near where I live in central Los Angeles. I trust it’ll take a year to settle in…

In what medium or media do you work (e.g., photography, sculpture, performance, etc.)?

I’ve always worked primarily in photography, with some projects in zine-making, bookmaking, photo-collage, and a few sculptures.

Describe your practice (e.g., conceptual, activist, curatorial, interdisciplinary, etc.), and when did you get started?

I’m an artist who makes photographs and related collage and, in the past, zine works. I did make some photo-sculptures in 2023-2025. I began making photographs in high school around 1998, and studied photography in college at NYU’s Tisch School of the Arts Photography and Imaging Department, 2000-2004. So I suppose I got started somewhere in there, but I would consider my first work that I’d be comfortable showing now, to be portraits made beginning in 2005.

©Paul Mpagi Sepuya, Darkroom Mirror (0X5A1531), 2017, pigment print, 34 x 51 inches. From DARK ROOM

In what directions have your projects evolved over time?

My projects have evolved in unexpected ways that I could not have anticipated. I began making portraits because I wanted to get to know, and to hold onto, various relationships and friendships when I was younger, and that has not stopped. But it has changed. The first portrait project created problems that shifted my perspective and introduced new questions, that became the next project. And so forth. And so it has gone. I try to respond in creative ways, and I do not plan projects that are then executed.

What types of investigations, methods and subject matter does your work explore?

I came to realize that my work is about the processes and complications from the production of portraiture in queer and homoerotic economies of exchange, and then became more and more about the medium of photography itself. Through all of this, I’ve pushed and questioned what it means to make a “black” image in unexpected ways, and how to approach the difficulty of eroticism and sex in photography that I want to be in conversation with broader subjects.

©Paul Mpagi Sepuya, Studio Mirror Position (_DSF7634), 2024, 18 x 24 inches. From TRANCE

Within which communities do you identify, and what audiences do you have in mind when producing work?

I think about my community of friends and that’s the only audience I can think of. Otherwise, I would be too shy to make anything. The equation changes when it comes to exhibition, but I have to start with myself in the process of making.

How long do your projects usually take?

Pictures and ideas develop into projects or bodies of work in their own time. I tend to have a larger “project” that’s made up of several or many interrelated bodies of work, that are articulated over several exhibitions. For example, DARK ROOM.

What level of visual literacy and art historical knowledge would you say is useful in understanding or appreciating your work?

I think it’s good to have a sense of 1990s pop and music culture as well as 1970s-2000s gay porn to get a context for my early portraits. The stripped down directness to them was a response I think, in 2005, to a kind of hyper production that I was drawn to as a teenager. It’s good to know the queer zine landscape of the aughts to get another sense of the community of friends and collaborators, and to understand the turn my work took around 2013, the big conceptual photography moment of the 2000s to about 2015. I really wanted to turn the “magic” of photography into a way of visualizing and representing queer experience and play. The Dark Room project with its mirrors was me wanting to engage in an explicitly erotic and hard-to-control way with Michael Fried’s arguments about absorption and theatricality. [Note: Absorption and Theatricality: Painting and Beholder in the Age of Diderot , Michael Fried, 1976.] But all of this is still very much complimented by what viewers bring to the work in unexpected ways.

©Paul Mpagi Sepuya, Daylight Studio (0X5A4718) [S13-03], 2022, salt print, 11 x 14 inches. From Daylight Studio / Dark Room Studio

I think that my first introduction to your images was seeing them circulated in

Butt

and maybe

Shoot

magazines. Within that context they functioned as an anchor and visual manifestation of a much wider community than I otherwise had access to at the time. How did you choose to print your projects early on, and has digital media changed that approach?

Both BUTT and my SHOOT zine emerged with the 2000s internet. My zine pointed to my website and blog, BUTT had their friendster-style magazine social media site. So yes, they both pointed toward community out there somewhere, if you didn’t know us/them. Many friends and collaborators were formed in those and intersecting spaces. I started making the zines in 2005 because I wanted to have fun. They were affordable, accessible, and felt special to make and people were excited to find them. My zines were very unelaborated, which I didn’t appreciate as a stand-out characteristic at the time. But I had a website long before I made zines. Since probably 1997, and I was also making and sharing photo prints with friends simultaneously. Digital media didn’t change my approach to zine-making. It was no longer having the time, with demands shifting to making and exhibiting prints. I keep thinking how nice it would be to get back to photo-copy machine zines. Now everything is professionally printed. I’m not sure if those are zines, even though I’ve made them.

Has the way your work circulates affected its cultural position and placement, or your methods?

I share much less of what I make, and hold work back but much longer than I did years ago. I made physical zines but as I mentioned earlier, I also scanned and posted on my website and WordPress blog almost every photograph I printed. Now I share very little work, maybe in the single digit percentage, preferring to only make available what is physically in exhibition.

©Paul Mpagi Sepuya, Daylight Studio (0X5A6854), 2022, 18 x 24 inches. from Daylight Studio / Dark Room Studio

Some of the descriptions of your exhibitions also bring to mind the pleasant sense of vertigo that I experience as a viewer in the middle of a Wolfgang Tillmans installation, in terms of how scale and sight lines make me question dimensions of where I am viscerally standing. Are curatorial strategies like these at play at different stages in your work?

Absolutely. I’ve heard Tillmans talk about his exhibition installation process and it’s fascinating to me because it’s so detailed. Of course things change, but it begins with a detailed process. I realize I can really only work with a sense of total volume of pictures and space, and then trust that there is enough nested information within the pictures that these relationships will be fun to re-encounter in the installation process. Sight lines between works, where subjects or fragments or different instances appear and re-appear, or an object that carries along across years, or accidental mirroring between pictures…

So yes, it’s in the work at different stages while making the work, anticipating its presentation, then re-discovered through attentiveness in the space of exhibition during installation. A lot of this information I’ve realized is something that only I see, or I tune into it because I have the narrative information that a viewer or curator does not have. But then when it comes together, it becomes tangible to others in the space.

©Paul Mpagi Sepuya, Mirror Study (0X5A6571), 2018. 34 x 51 inches. From Mirror Studies

How does your current survey exhibition at the Sprengel Museum in Hanover personally compare to your 2019 survey (of 2006-2018 work) at the Contemporary Art Museum in St. Louis—in terms of dialog around subject and object relations, facets of the gaze, hunches, investigations, and historicity?

The CAM St. Louis show was the first big presentation of the DARK ROOM project, which at the time was about three years in. I had made a significant amount of work in the interconnected series there, and it was anchored by earlier projects—portraits, zines, Studio Museum residency work. But it really felt like a work laying out possibilities of what was to come. The historicity of this new exhibition is overwhelming, honestly, because it’s coincided with moving on. I wanted to make an argument with the first show that my UCLA Thesis work and the new Dark Room series emerged from a deeper investment and community, when there were some upsetting moments trying to frame those as my “first” exhibitions and first works. I had been making work for 15 years at that point. Focus. Desire. is an exhibition of what I have done, and opens up space for me to not know yet what comes next.

[Sprengel Museum’s press release describes the show: From July 1 through October 4, 2026, the Sprengel Museum Hannover presents “Paul Mpagi Sepuya. Focus. Desire,” the first major solo museum exhibition in Germany dedicated to the work of American photographer Paul Mpagi Sepuya… Developed in collaboration with Fotomuseum Winterthur, the exhibition brings together early and recent bodies of work alongside materials from the artist’s personal archive. Curator Stefan Gronert explains: “In Sepuya’s work, the image does not emerge from a singular gaze or a fixed perspective, but from relationships—between bodies, camera, space, mirrors, and ultimately the viewer. It is these connections that bring the image into being in the first place.”]

Aspects of hide and seek, performance and narrativity, cruising and mirroring, etc. elicits an experience of yearning and give-and-take, for me, in viewing various bodies of your work. How conscious are you of these considerations while you’re in the process of making the work?

These are definitely at the forefront, and are a big part of that process. I would have to think about what something like “cruising” might look like if translated to a photograph structurally and compositionally, and then balance that setup with something completely unpredictable and dynamic. It’s a pleasurable and extended and sometimes head-trippy process. To think formally is to be outside of the picture, and to produce the work, there has to be a letting go and being present in excess..

©Paul Mpagi Sepuya, Night Studio Mirror (DSF1073), 2024, dye-sublimation on aluminum in aluminum artist frame, 19.5 x 24.5 inches. From TRANCE

Unless noted, all works pigment prints. All works courtesy the artist, Vielmetter Los Angeles, DOCUMENT, Chicago, Bortolami, New York, and Galerie Peter Kilchmann, Zürich and Paris.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : Tony Revolori ( Primetime ), Audrina Miranda ( Jurassic World Rebirth ), Maria Gabriella de Faria ( Superman ) and Lou Lou Safran ( Shazam ) are set to star in coming-of-age indie movie Night At The Oasis , which will shoot on 35mm.

Written and directed by Kim Caicedo, cast also includes Marcela Carvajal, Alysia Reiner, Connor Apolo, Ken Kirby, Noen Perez, and Nishta Cattinari.

Filming is being lined up for this winter on the movie which is based on real events and will follow “an eleven year old girl named Lilly (Miranda) who must learn to navigate the world by herself when she is accidentally left behind at a gas station while traveling with her truck-driver father (Revolori).

Related Stories

Odette Annable To Topline Psychological Horror Film 'Anima' From Andrés Beltrán

Tony Revolori Signs With Verve

Stated Caicedo: “This story came from real life, which is wonderful for storytelling and terrible for the people who have to live it. I wanted to honor that experience without losing the humor and messiness that make it real.”

Watch on Deadline

The project is getting support from the LA and Atlanta Kodak teams, as well as Panavision. Jessica Arzate will be DoP.

“Shooting on film feels right for this story because I want the images to have a pulse, the feeling that you’re looking at a memory, unpredictable, and impossible to rewind like life is.” said Caicedo.

Pic is being produced by Heliya Alam of LBM Pictures, Warner Davis of Hemlock Circle Productions, Caijo Films, alongside Alvaro Gutierrez of Agora Films and Nicolas Troya of Troya Films. Tony Revolori is also producing.

article_text:
For director Jennifer Peedom , bringing the story of Tenzing Norgay to the screen meant more than re-creating one of mountaineering’s most celebrated achievements. It also meant putting the Himalayan climber at the center of his own story and taking audiences onto real mountains to experience the dangers of the ascent.

Tenzing , written by Luke Davies, chronicles Norgay’s ( Genden Phuntsok ) journey to the summit of Mount Everest alongside New Zealand mountaineer Edmund Hillary ( Tom Hiddleston ) in 1953, drawing on more than two decades of Peedom’s experience filming in the Himalayas to make her first narrative feature. Speaking recently at PMC Studios’ Lumen West screening theater, the filmmaker discussed the production’s demanding locations, her transition from documentary filmmaking and the responsibility of telling a story that accounts of Hillary’s achievement have often overshadowed.

Related Stories

‘Tenzing’ Review: Tom Hiddleston Stars In Story Of First Successful Expedition To Peak Of Mount Everest, But It Is Really All About The Sherpa – Telluride Film Festival

‘Tenzing’ Trailer: Tom Hiddleston, WIllem Dafoe, Genden Phuntsok, Class, Ambition & The Battle To Conquer Mount Everest

“I wanted to tell the story of Tenzing Norgay, but I knew that it couldn’t be told as a documentary,” Peedom said. “None of the story that you see in the past of his childhood and the love story and the epic kind of obstacles that he had to overcome just to get to the starting line had been documented in any way.”

Peedom previously directed Sherpa , her 2015 documentary that followed an Everest expedition from the Sherpas’ perspective. During production, an avalanche killed 16 Sherpas in the icefall, turning the film into a chronicle of the disaster and the disproportionate risks Himalayan climbers take while helping foreign mountaineers pursue their ambitions.

That experience, along with years of relationships in the region, ultimately helped lead Norgay’s family to entrust Peedom with his story. Moving into narrative filmmaking allowed her to explore the climber’s life beyond the historical record, while collaborating with actors and craftspeople to bring his journey to the screen. “I found that the skills that I had learned, the powers of observation of human behavior, and when you know something’s truthful [and] when you’re working with actors, you have these collaborators that you can work with to enhance performance,” Peedom said.

One of Peedom’s most consequential decisions was to shoot the film’s climbing sequences on real mountains rather than rely on green screens. The production filmed its ice-and-snow scenes in New Zealand’s Southern Alps during winter, with locations accessible only by helicopter. The conditions required small crews and short shooting days.

Peedom worked with New Zealand mountain guide Guy Cotter, who had climbed Everest five times, to identify locations that could stand in for the Khumbu Icefall, Everest’s summit and Hillary Step. A second unit also filmed on Everest itself, capturing the deep backgrounds that visual effects artists later combined with the New Zealand footage. “I just kept pushing that idea until no one came up with a good enough answer to tell me why I couldn’t do it,” she said of her determination to film on real terrain.

Authenticity extended to the cast. Peedom also arranged for the lead actors to spend time in the Himalayas, where Phuntsok could immerse himself in Sherpa culture and dialect. At the same time, Hiddleston built a rapport and took walks with Hillary’s grandson, Alexander, to experience the landscape and better understand the historical partnership.

For Peedom, the film’s cultural and historical context was just as important as its physical scale. Norgay’s story explores the tensions of class, colonial power and competing ambitions, while presenting the climbers as equals whose achievement depended on mutual respect. “Tenzing was a Himalayan mountaineer. [He and Hillary] were equals,” Peedom said. “And this is a story about what happens when two people can meet each other as equals and achieve something together with respect.”

That perspective is reflected in the film’s title. Rather than framing Norgay primarily through his association with Hillary, Peedom wanted his name to stand on its own. “Tenzing is described as the Sherpa guide. They don’t even mostly use his name, which is why I wanted to call the movie Tenzing . For all of you to know the great [work] he has done.”

Watch the video above for more insights on the behind-the-scenes making of Tenzing for Deadline’s screening series.

Tenzing is now available to watch on Apple TV.

article_text:
Japanese director Sho Miyake , whose “Two Seasons, Two Strangers” won the Golden Leopard at Locarno in 2025, will get his first North American retrospective at New York’s Metrograph from Nov. 7–17. It is one stop on a Japan Foundation tour of 14 cities in eight countries.

The Metrograph program, titled “Unspoken Gestures: The Films of Sho Miyake,” is co-organized and presented by the Japan Foundation. Miyake will attend in person over the opening weekend, and select encore screenings will follow the main run.

Related Stories

Hulu's Mother-Son Mystery 'Phony' Mutes Connie Britton's Charisma Under Visual Effects: TV Review

The series brings together eight of Miyake’s own titles. They include his 2012 debut feature “Playback,” which premiered at Locarno, and “The Cockpit” (2014), a 64-minute film that watches producer-rapper OMSB and his collaborator Bim make a track in a small suburban Tokyo apartment. “And Your Bird Can Sing” (2018) screens with the 2016 short “August 8th,” and “Two Seasons, Two Strangers” is paired with the 2016 short “Nagahama.” Boxing drama “Small, Slow but Steady” (2022) and “All the Long Nights” (2024) round out the lineup.

Popular on Variety

Miyake has also picked two films that influenced his work as carte blanche selections: David Elfick’s 1973 surf film “Crystal Voyager” and Aoyama Shinji’s 2007 drama “Sad Vacation,” the final part of Aoyama’s “Kitakyushu Saga,” starring Asano Tadanobu. He will introduce both on Nov. 8, after Q&As following “Small, Slow but Steady” and “Two Seasons, Two Strangers” the day before.

“For a long time now, Sho Miyake has been one of international cinema’s best-kept secrets, each of his films landing quietly but forcefully amid the cacophony of contemporary film culture. With this retrospective, we’re giving the man a microphone and calling on New York audiences to attend the voice of an essential Japanese film artist,” said Metrograph programmer Edo Choi.

The tour opens on Nov. 3 in Washington, D.C., where the Japan Information & Culture Center at the Embassy of Japan will screen “Two Seasons, Two Strangers” and Miyake will join the Q&A remotely. Oklahoma follows from Nov. 9–11, with screenings at the University of Oklahoma’s Meacham Auditorium in Norman and the Oklahoma City Museum of Art. Miyake will also teach a masterclass for a university screenwriting class that is closed to the public.

Los Angeles hosts the program Nov. 13–15 at the Japan Foundation, Los Angeles, UCR Arts at the University of California, Riverside, and the American Cinematheque’s Los Feliz Theatre. The lineup there adds King Vidor’s “The Patsy” (1928) and Tony Scott’s “Deja Vu” (2006). Toronto runs Nov. 17–19 at TIFF Bell Lightbox, the Fox Theatre and Paradise Cinema, with Miyake’s 2010 film “Good for Nothing” and Jacques Demy’s “Bay of Angels” (1962) on the bill.

In the new year, the tour heads to Paris, Toulouse, Rome, Turin, Madrid, Zurich, Cologne, London and Derby, and wraps in February 2027. Miyake will travel to every city except Washington.

In a joint statement, Inoue Ryo and Rokkaku Akinaru of the Japan Foundation pointed to Miyake’s own description of a director’s job as “taking on the responsibility of creating images of humanity.”

“We, too, are among the audience members who were once struck and moved by his gaze. We sincerely hope to bring that sense of wonder and emotion to as many viewers as possible in theaters around the world,” they said.

Miyake made “Playback” while still in his mid-twenties. Murakami Jun plays an actor nearing 40 who wakes up on the way to a hometown wedding wearing his old school uniform. His friend Hamaguchi Ryusuke compared the film to “a modern-day reincarnation of [John Cassavetes’s] ‘Opening Night.’”

“Small, Slow but Steady” stars Kishii Yukino and is drawn from the life of deaf boxer Ogasawara Keiko. “All the Long Nights,” adapted from Seo Maiko’s novel, pairs Matsumura Hokuto and Kamishiraishi Mone as co-workers who form a bond. “Two Seasons, Two Strangers” adapts two manga by Tsuge Yoshiharu and stars Kawai Yuumi, Takada Mansaku, Shim Eun-kyung and Tsutsumi Shinichi.

article_text:
Bollywood filmmaker Vikas Bahl has finished filming in the U.K. on “ Bolo Bolo Bolo ,” a coming-of-age musical drama set during the boom in Punjabi music across Britain in the early 1990s.

Jimmy Shergill , Siddhant Chaturvedi , Mona Singh and Alizeh lead the cast. Katha Studios is producing the film alongside Good Co, Fusion Flicks and Monk Films. It will open in cinemas in 2027.

The story takes place at a time when young British musicians were mixing Punjabi beats with modern, bass-heavy production. They built that sound in makeshift spaces, from garages to unlicensed radio broadcasts and shows far from the mainstream circuit. Alongside the music, the film deals with family ties, friendship, identity and the search for belonging, against the backdrop of Britain’s shifting culture at the time.

Related Stories

Quentin Tarantino Surprises Fans With 17 Minutes of ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ at AFI Fest

Quentin Tarantino Confirms He's ‘Written a Script’ for His Tenth Film, But Won’t Pursue It Yet Because He Wants to ‘Live a Little’

Shibasish Sarkar, founder of Katha Studios, said: “‘Bolo Bolo Bolo’ captures a unique cultural movement that brought together music, identity and a generation finding its voice. The film explores a fascinating chapter in the evolution of Punjabi music in Britain, and we are excited to bring this story to audiences. With Vikas Bahl at the helm and a talented ensemble cast, we look forward to the film’s release in 2027.”

The soundtrack covers a wide range, drawing on the sounds that drove the British Punjabi scene during that decade.

Bahl said the film centers on music, identity and belonging, and takes place in a period when a generation was forging a cultural identity of its own.

“The Punjabi music scene in 1990s Britain was full of energy, rebellion and an incredible spirit of self-expression,” Bahl said. “It has been a wonderful experience bringing this world to life, and I look forward to audiences experiencing the film in 2027.”

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Greenwich Entertainment has acquired North American rights to Big Break , a comedic thriller marking the debut feature of New York-based sketch comedy group Simple Town . They’ll release the film in theaters across the country next year.

From the producers of If I Had Legs I’d Kick You , The History of Concrete and Good One , Big Break is set years after a fictionalized version of Simple Town has disbanded. Old friends Will (Will Niedmann), Caroline (Caro Yost) and Felipe (Felipe Di Poi Tamargo) reunite with their estranged ex-collaborator Sam (Samuel Lanier), the only one of them to have become successful in Hollywood for heralding box office smash hit The Gummy Bears Movie , for a nostalgic weekend reunion at his secluded mansion in the woods. While the three try to devise a plan to get cast in Sam’s upcoming sequel, dark secrets are revealed, and these washed-up comedians learn what it really means to kill.

Related Stories

CAA Signs Bloodline Banter Comedy Duo

Comedian Ron Funches Signs With Artists First

World premiering over the summer at Fantasia Film Festival, Big Break is directed by Ian Faria, who worked from a script by Lanier. Additional cast includes Ivy Wolk and Jefferson White.

Watch on Deadline

Formed in 2016, Simple Town has carved out a niche as an alt-comedy favorite. They’re known for their self-aware takes on viral internet content, cinematic short films, and live tours in the U.S. and UK. Big Break highlights the style and chemistry they’ve developed through 10 years of collaboration.

The group said in a joint statement, “We are so excited to work with Greenwich Entertainment on the release of our first feature. It’s a comedy, it’s a slasher, it’s a movie about our real and dire friendship. We can’t wait for audiences to see it big and loud in a packed movie theater.”

Big Break was produced by Sarah Wilson, Ani Schroeter, Graham Mason, Richie Doyle and Conor Hannon. The acquisition was negotiated by Greenwich’s Jasper Basch with CAA Media Finance representing the filmmakers. Simple Town is represented by WME, as well as Allen McRae at Authentic Talent and Literary Management.

To get Deadline’s Comedy Means Business newsletter, covering all things comedy, in your inbox, sign up here .

article_text:
Everybody to Kenmure Street ’s bid for Oscar recognition is gaining traction. The film directed by Felipe Bustos Sierra earned a spot on the influential DOC NYC short list of the year’s best documentaries announced on Wednesday. And on Tuesday, the film from executive producer Emma Thompson earned four nominations for the Critics Choice Documentary Awards , including Best Documentary Feature and Best Director.

Bustos Sierra’s film captures a remarkable event that took place in Glasgow, Scotland on May 13, 2021. Early that morning, immigration enforcement agents from the Home Office attempted to grab two Sikh men in a dawn raid but when locals became aware of what was going on they intervened, leading to an extraordinary standoff between law enforcement and members of the community in and around Kenmure Street.

Related Stories

Doc Talk Podcast: Producer James Costa On Deadline’s For The Love Of Docs Series, Oscar Season And ‘NAZA’ Controversy

Uniformed officers probably were unaware of the history of that neighborhood and of Glasgow as a whole and how residents there view immigrants.

Watch on Deadline

“This is a welcoming place… The south side of Glasgow has been a landing space for immigrants for centuries, since it was created really, [with] working class and immigrants living together,” the filmmaker said after a screening of the film as part of Deadline’s For the Love of Docs event series. “Glasgow has always been seen as a bit of a rebel city… And that history obviously permeates that neighborhood.”

The first person to try to disrupt the attempted immigration raid came to be known as “Van Man.” That individual climbed under the immigration vehicle in which the detainees were being held and latched onto the rear axle. Eventually, as word spread, hundreds of people poured into the street, many recording the events with their cell phone cameras. It became an enormous undertaking for Bustos Sierra and his editor Colin Monie to synchronize all that footage.

“It was the hardest part of making this film,” Bustos Sierra conceded. “The entire protest is shown… through what people had at hand on the day. We were lucky that two people who lived on the street were professional cameramen and they started filming on the smartphones, but… they went back, got their 4K cameras and managed to capture the second half of the day. But most of it is smartphone cameras and some really bad, some really old ones too.”

He added that some of the video came from activists who had scrubbed the metadata, “which made it really difficult to create an accurate timeline, which we eventually got to, but that was months of work.”

Emma Thompson not only executive produced the film, but she stars in it, in a manner of speaking — playing Van Man. That inventive choice came about after the real van man (who preferred to remain anonymous) said his words from interviews with the director could be used in the film, but he didn’t want to appear in it himself.

“Luckily, I had kept a light correspondence with Emma Thompson after my first film came out about Chile, a country that she has also a strong connection with,” Bustos Sierra explained. “And so, when Van Man told me didn’t want to be in it… you think, ‘What do I have?’ …And I just pictured Emma Thompson going out there and saying, ‘Hey, I’m Van Man.’ It made me laugh like maybe what Van Man did [for] the protest, Emma will do for our film.”

The dramatized sequence, shot in London, involved Thompson climbing onto a rig beneath a van. She was wedged in there like the real guy in Glasgow.

“We did build the rig. We did put her under underneath the van. When she did arrive, she looked at the rig, looked at me and [cinematographer] Kirsten [McMahon] and say, ‘This is the strangest thing anyone’s ever asked me to do.’ …I think she made the discomfort part of her performance. And so, it worked really well.”

Bustos Sierra sees what the people around Kenmure Street did that day as “small revolutionary acts.” He describes their attitude as, “You don’t remove [these men] without valid cause as this was happening. There’s absolutely nothing illegal [done] by these two guys. These are our neighbors and we’re just going to stand for our community.”

Watch the full conversation in the video above.

For The Love of Docs is produced with the long-time support of National Geographic Documentary Films . Films are presented free of charge to the audience and to the filmmakers. The series continues with weekly screenings, followed by conversations with filmmakers through December 1.
